utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-87-A, the Prosecutor versus Nikola Sainovic, Nebojsa Pavkovic, Vladimir Lazarevic, and Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As indicated, if any party is unable to follow the proceedings at any stage, I ask them to bring this to my attention immediately. May I now have the appearances of the parties. The Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. The Prosecution counsel this morning are myself, joined by Daniela Kravetz and Mr. Kyle Wood, assisting us again is Mr. Colin Nawrot, our case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now the Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Toma Fila, and together with Mr. Petrovic I represent the Defence of Nikola Sainovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman and along with Aleksander Aleksic we represent General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Mihajlo Bakrac. For the Defence of General Lazarevic I am here with my colleague, Mr. Cepic, and our intern, Mr. Milan Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Dan Ivetic on behalf of Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Today we will hear the submissions from the counsel for Mr. Lukic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, honoured members of panel. My name is again Branko Lukic with counsel for Mr. Sreten Lukic. By way of introduction I want to let you know that we will be devoting time to focus our presentation to the five questions that Your Honours posed to us, and we will incorporate them into discussions about our appeal where appropriate. I wish to advise that we will be dealing with all five questions. First of all, I want to point out this judgement convicted Lukic and gave him a harsh sentence of 22 years which is astounding when the same judgement clears him of responsibility for many parts of the Prosecution case against him. In book III, paragraph 85, he is shown not to be specially promoted as Milosevic's inner circle. In book III, paragraph 1072, he is shown not to have been involved in violations of the October Accords. In book III, 1015, it is shown that he is not in charge of the work of the RDB, state security part of MUP, even though the main document, P1505, cited by the Chamber and relied upon throughout the judgement lists RDB staff as being subordinated to him. In book III, 1075, it is shown that Lukic did not have authority over border police stations. In book III, 1051, it is shown that Lukic did not replace Obrad Stevanovic or Vlastimir Djordjevic or any of the existing police hierarchy. In book III, 1113, it is shown that Lukic was not involved in the clandestine attempt to transport and hide corpses from Kosovo. Book III, 1021, it is confirmed that Lukic did not participate in the drafting of the global plan for the suppression of terrorism. In book III, 1049, it is concluded that Lukic could not commence or proceed with disciplinary actions against MUP members. In book III, 1122, it is shown that there were no volunteers operating within the MUP. In addition to these factors which the Trial Chamber here found, we wish to direct your attention to the facts that there were three main phases in 1998 and 1999 that were different from each other. The first phase was the one of anti-terrorist actions in 1998. During that period, both head of the public security and Deputy Minister Djordjevic as well as assistant minister and PJP commander Obrad Stevanovic were in Kosovo the entire time. After that is the phase of the signed peace accords in 1998 and 1999. With the NATO bombings the third phase begins, in which again the factual and legal framework changed. The Prosecution and the judgement do not recognise these different phases which then leads to improper legal conclusions. Everyone with logic would know that the war brings a new set of circumstances and laws into play. Further, during this period assistant minister Obrad Stevanovic, the PJP commander, came to Kosovo immediately before the NATO bombing with PJP units, and stayed there for the duration, signing the Kumanovo Agreement and was among the last policemen to leave Kosovo upon the withdrawal. Now I wish to address the first question you posed before turning the podium over to my co-counsel, Mr. Ivetic. The question was whether there would be any effect on Lukic's appeal regarding his convictions pursuant to JCE III if the Appeals Chamber were to accept the Prosecution's argument that the Trial Chamber applied an incorrect mens rea standard to JCE III liability. Having in mind that this question has been addressed already by all those that have gone before us, we will be brief. We do not believe that the resolution of the Prosecution appeal as to the mens rea standard for JCE III affects our appeal. We believe our client was wrongly convicted under either standard and we believe the factual scenario under the evidence supports an acquittal under both standards. We submit that upon a review of our submissions hopefully Your Honours will see that the judgement is full of errors and cannot stand on its own. It falls apart with any degree of scrutiny applied. Such a judgement is unsafe and we believe your intervention is required to prevent a serious miscarriage of justice. And now I give the floor to my co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the record, I am Dan Ivetic. Your Honours have posed a question about the evidence, if any, relating to Sreten Lukic's involvement in the disarming of the Kosovo Albanian population. In this regard, it should be noted that in book III dealing with the individual responsibility of Mr. Lukic, the Trial Chamber fails to analyse the evidence as to this disarming. Rather, only in book III, paragraph 666, dealing with another appellant, the Trial Chamber claims that the disarming process was in furtherance of the aims of the JCE. Further, at paragraph 668, the trial judgement merely states that: "The MUP undertook the task of disarming Kosovo Albanians in the interior of the province, Pavkovic ordered that the Pristina Corps carry this out in the border belt." There is no citation to the evidence or any discussion of the evidence on which this assertion as to the MUP is based. Apart from P1468, notes of the meeting where it is suggested that the MUP should undertake this task and Lukic's response is recorded in English as mostly illegible. Surely this is not evidence to sustain a conviction. There is no inference that the disarming suggested at this meeting was ever undertaken or that it involved Lukic. Further, the B/C/S original confirms that Lukic's response dealt solely with voluntary surrender of arms. Despite not discussing any evidence as to Lukic, in paragraph 1121 of book III, the Chamber concludes: "In 1998 Lukic was actively involved in ... the disarming of the Kosovo Albanian population in villages and towns in the province." But again, the Chamber does not cite or discuss any evidence. A look at the evidence, Your Honours, shows important distinctions must be made. As a starting point, we would ask that the Chamber focus on what type of disarming is at issue. Long before the Kosovo conflict and certainly at least since 1992, there existed in Serbia, including the province of Kosovo, a Law on Weapons and Ammunition, Article 33 of which prohibited civilians from possessing illegal types of weapons and which proscribed penalties for such possession. This is in evidence at P1016, page 119. This law applied uniformly to the entirety of Serbia and cannot be said to be discriminatory in nature. Lukic cannot be said to have had any role in the promulgation of this law, active or otherwise. Your Honours, the law is reasonable and it makes sense. I dare say that most countries have a similar law and most of them task the police with enforcing it. As to this specific law, the minister of internal affairs set forth how this law was to be enforced and implemented, not Sreten Lukic. Indeed, the evidence shows that in 1996, long before the indictment period, the minister gave an instruction on the work of internal organs within the public security sector. And this is P1239. Section II of the same at point 17 lists item 2: Prevention and detection of abuses of weapons, the detection and seizure of arms held without permits. Also in evidence we see that the SUPs, or secretariats of the interior, across the whole of Serbia created plans for their functioning every year, including tasks aimed at enforcing this law, among others. An example of one such plan is P1074. As is clear from this, Sreten Lukic had no role in either enacting the law, promulgating instructions on its enforcement, nor in planning how the SUPs were to police the law. Now, if we turn to the time-period of 1998, we will see at that time the evidence shows that as part of the effort to reduce tensions an amnesty had been declared by the government organs of both Serbia and the provincial organs of Kosovo to call upon and allow citizens who had been forced to take up illegal arms by the KLA to voluntarily surrender those illegal arms without suffering the legal consequences that otherwise would apply under the law. The judgement only links this to the testimony of Veljko Odalovic in paragraph 70 of book III, but the evidence, namely P908, Article 5, item 3, demonstrates that this was decreed by the National Assembly of Serbia in the last quarter of 1998 for everyone. Again, there is no role of Lukic in promulgating this amnesty. Now, the judgement has focused on reports that allegedly do not mention that the weapons being collected by the MUP were illegal weapons under this programme, at book III, paragraph 70. A review of the evidence demonstrates that P1198 and P1203 are the only such reports, and both documents in pages 4 and 5 respectively talk of the MUP involvement in taking custody only of weapons voluntarily surrendered by citizens. It is a reasonable conclusion under the facts that this was part of the amnesty and the law which the Trial Chamber does not exclude. Now, it stands to reason that police organs would be involved in securing custody of and documenting such illegal weapons that were voluntarily surrendered by citizens. This is a normal task in any country. Looking at what role Lukic played in all of this, we see that he is only reporting the statistics of numbers and locations of such weapons that were surrendered. This can be seen from P1468, where we see the direct references to weapons taken into custody by the MUP after they were voluntarily surrendered by civilians at entries for 8 August 1998, 26 August 1998, 6 September 1998, 7 September 1998, 10 September 1998, 12 September 1998, 13 September 1998, and 14 September 1998. All these entries are merely Lukic reporting statistics of instances where a couple of persons or groups voluntarily surrendered weapons of a few in number, up to 200 in number. Again, Lukic is neither promulgating the tasks nor effectuating the surrender of illegal arms, but is merely reporting the statistics as to persons who have voluntarily surrendered their arms to the police. Further, that these arms are illegal in nature can be seen from the fact that they include even Armburst anti-tank launchers. Thus, the Trial Chamber's earlier finding that these voluntary collections were not in reference to illegal arms is in error. From such a limited involvement in a completely legal enterprise, Lukic cannot be said to have the necessary mens rea to be assisting in any criminal enterprise. In this regard, not only was the voluntary surrender of arms obligated by the law, it was supported by international peace initiatives. Specifically, UN Security Council Resolution 1160, dated 31 March 1998 and in evidence as P455, identified the KLA as a terrorist organisation and prohibited the procurement of weapons by either individuals or other groups in Kosovo in order to stem terrorist activities. This initiative cannot be said to be discriminatory. Further, it is dated two months before Lukic even came to Kosovo. As is evidenced by P1468 at page 43, Shaun Byrnes, the head of the US KDOM mission, was involved in this legal process, keeping track of the weapons and villages involved, asking for such statistics and information from Lukic and being provided the same. Thus, the highest-ranking member of the international community in Kosovo was fully apprised of and involved in the reporting by Lukic of the voluntary surrender of weapons. The voluntary surrender of arms was in the interest of all persons and parties interested in pursuing peace in the region. This is the only participation of Lukic that can be inferred from the evidence. Given the involvement of the international community in these efforts and the oversight of Mr. Byrnes in Lukic's reporting, it is illogical and simply unsupportable under any reading of the evidence to conclude that Lukic had knowledge of any criminal enterprise behind these actions. From this evidence it is inconceivable to conclude that Lukic was engaged in any "disarming" of the Kosovo Albanian population with the intent to further the criminal aims of any criminal enterprise. In reaching such conclusions unsupported by the evidence, the Trial Chamber erred; and we therefore ask the assistance of this Chamber to correct those errors and render a just result. Surely we do not want to send a message to the world that a policeman reporting statistics of voluntary illegal weapons surrendered that was proscribed by domestic law, supported by the UN Security Council and by international diplomats, should be guilty of a crime for the same. Otherwise, we would have the absurd result that the citizen voluntarily surrendering arms is also guilty of the JCE, as are the members of the Security Council calling for a conflicted area to turn over illegally held weapons. At this time, we take the opportunity to address a related topic, namely, the arming of the non-Albanian population. In the judgement the Chamber always links this activity with the process of disarming which we have just discussed; that can be seen in book III, paragraphs 49, 72, 666 through 669, and at several other places. But they are not the same. Whereas the collection of voluntarily surrendered weapons dealt with illegal weapons, the process of arming did not deal with illegal weapons but rather was a process that was legal in nature and involved the legitimate distribution of arms to reserve defence formations of the state that were being activated in the light of an impending war. The judgement itself concludes at book III, paragraph 56, that it was unable to conclude whether such arming was illegal per se, but considers that the primary issue is whether it was done upon ethnic lines. Again, any involvement in a legal activity in compliance with the existing laws surely cannot be used as the sole basis to conclude that one had criminal intent and knew of or supported a criminal enterprise behind these legal activities. Further, the judgement's focus on the ethnic lines is curious given that the Chamber was shown and concluded that Kosovo Albanian citizens rejected participating in the work of official state organs. We can see that from book III, paragraphs 225, 226, and 297. And based on the evidence the Chamber could see that any perceived co-operation with the state authorities by Kosovo Albanians was denounced as collaboration by the KLA and subjected such persons to reprisals by this criminal group including murders. And the evidence of that is discussed at paragraphs 537 through 543 of our appeal. With such a factual background, any attempted distribution of arms to any ethnic Albanian Yugoslav reservists would have been devoid of logic. This is an alternative meaning that the Trial Chamber ignored and did so in error. Although the judgement repeatedly talks of a secret arming process - that can be seen in book III, paragraphs 52, 64, 72, 1121 - there is no evidence that Lukic participated in any such secret process. Indeed, the first and only time in the judgement where the moniker secret is applied to Lukic's involvement is at book III, paragraph 1121, when it is making conclusions as to his criminal responsibility. The previous paragraphs, 1060, 1067, 1071, talking about the evidence do not relate to any secret arming of civilians but rather the arming of reserve police formations, civil protection units and army reservists in accord with the laws of the state. The arming of defence formations must be understood under the wider context of events at the time. The KLA was increasing the intensity of terrorist attacks at the time and it was becoming a possibility that NATO would attack Yugoslavia, making activation of the reserve defence formations logical and legal, without any connotation of any criminal enterprise. The Chamber failed to consider the evidence that the Supreme Defence Council issued an order 21 May 1998 for reservists to be armed - that's P1259 - and that Lukic had no role in the bringing of this decision which was brought by the highest organ of the state and which he was duty-bound to implement once Minister Stojiljkovic issued an instruction to engage the reserve force of the police in June 1998. And we see that from the testimony of Cvetic at T.8169. Such actions were in accord with the Law of Defence, which is P985, and the Law on Internal Affairs, which is P1737, Article 28, such that Lukic's involvement in this public process could not be termed as either illegal or nefarious. Thus, the Trial Chamber erred in finding that the only reasonable inference from the evidence was that Lukic knew of a criminal intent behind the arming of reservists and that he shared the same. Now I will address the third question posed by the Chamber to us which asked if the actus reus and mens rea for a JCE member can be fulfilled prior to the existence of the common purpose of the JCE. In short, Your Honours, our answer is no. The jurisprudence of the Tribunal is clear when it continuously affirms that the common purpose of a JCE does not need to be previously formulated but can materialise extemporaneously. We see that from the Furundzija appeal judgement, paragraph 119 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: However, the logical caveat of this finding is that the materialisation of the common purpose, i.e., its revelation or surface to the public is not the same thing as its prior existence which remains a precondition to the existence of a JCE I. A person accused of participating in a JCE category I must act in the implementation of a common purpose through acts directed to the furthering of the same. We see that from the Kvocka appeal judgement, paragraph 187, and the Vasiljevic appeal judgement, paragraph 102. The Defence cannot accept that both actus reus and mens rea of a JCE I could be fulfilled prior to the existence of the common purpose because that would amount to accepting that a JCE I extends abusively to any person who acted without any knowledge and intention to further something that simply did not exist at the time that he acted. If the Prosecution fails to provide evidence that can only be interpreted by the Chamber as proving the existence of a common purpose for a JCE, the Trial Chamber must not interpret other portions of evidence for the purposes of constructing the existence of a criminal purpose, since this would result in the Chamber erring in the determination of facts unduly affecting the accused. The Defence draws the attention of the Chamber to the findings of the Appeals Chamber in the Gotovina appeals judgement when determining that the Trial Chamber erred when finding the existence of a JCE I through the interpretation of evidence regarding the planning phase of an attack in light of subsequent events of the attack and its characterisation by that Chamber as being unlawful in nature. This is paragraph 93. In that case, the Appeals Chamber addressed the error of the Trial Chamber and said considered outside this erroneous retroactive context, it was not reasonable to find that the only possible interpretation of the Brioni transcript involved a JCE to forcibly deport Serb civilians. The Appeals Chamber highlighted many legitimate reasons civilians may leave a combat zone, including a lawful consensus in helping civilians leave an area of conflict for casualty reductions and legitimate military advantage and lawful combat operations. The error in Gotovina was remedied by acquittal. It is respectfully submitted a similar analysis is required here. Moving along to the fourth question that Your Honours posed, you asked under what circumstances the mens rea under JCE I for deportation and forcible transfers may be inferred from the accused's knowledge of crimes committed in 1998, including crimes other than deportation and forcible transfers. Our brief answer is that the mens rea cannot be inferred from knowledge of other crimes in 1998 that are not the same as those in 1999 for which the appellant is convicted. First I will address our legal submission and then apply the relevant facts from the evidence to demonstrate the error of such an approach, at least towards Mr. Lukic. The jurisprudence of the Tribunal is clear on the fact that members of the JCE I must share the same criminal intent - we can see that from the Krnojelac appeal judgement, paragraph 84; the Vasiljevic appeal judgement, paragraph 101 - and that the common plan was executed with the intent to commit a particular crime. We can see that from the Stakic appeals judgement, paragraph 65; the Vasiljevic Appeals Chamber judgement, paragraph 101, among others. In this sense the Defence believes that mere knowledge of previous crimes is not sufficient to infer the mens rea for JCE I, since this knowledge of forced transfer and deportations has not been proven to be the only reasonable conclusion for establishing criminal intent to pursue a common criminal goal. No weight was given to the fact that as a MUP officer, the allegations of potential crimes being committed by known and unknown perpetrators were part of Lukic's function as a policeman and only require his attention if other organs do not seem to be investigating them under the law. The mere knowledge of unconfirmed crimes does not necessarily lead to the conclusion that Lukic knew of the existence of a criminal common purpose behind those crimes, that their commission intended to further a criminal common purpose, or that he willingly decided to join the same, sharing such a goal in the future. Knowledge of other types of crimes that have no apparent connection to the alleged Serb plan to control Kosovo through the forcible removal of the Albanian population, such as murder and sexual assaults, are commonly investigated as normal crimes by police personnel around the world and do not show intent to pursue either a different crime, like forcible removal, nor take part in furthering a criminal policy of control. This is especially true where the knowledge of the accused is accompanied with assurances that the relevant authorities are conducting investigations to preserve evidence, locate and apprehend perpetrators for prosecution. We believe that the knowledge of a policeman that certain crimes were committed cannot be the sole basis for concluding the mens rea has been fulfilled for a JCE, for if that were the case every policeman on the plant would ipso facto be guilty of a JCE just by virtue of doing his job as a policeman investigating crimes. In this instant case the evidence is clear that there was no mens rea that could be inferred from incidents and crimes in 1998 that would lead to the sole reasonable conclusion that the crime of deportation and forcible transfer as part of a JCE was underway or intended by Lukic in 1999. The sole instance of murder that was relied upon in the judgement from 1998 as providing notice to the appellant was Gornje Obrinje, for which in paragraph 1134 of book III the Chamber said that it was the key evidence that Lukic knew that the police would commit crimes if it was again utilised in 1999. Not a single bit of evidence demonstrates that murder was established in Gornje Obrinje or that Lukic, as a policeman, could consider that murder had been established and the identity of perpetrators had been established. The Human Rights Watch publication on Gornje Obrinje was only written in 1999 - and that's at paragraph 900 of book I of the judgement - and there is no evidence it was sent to Lukic before or during the war. It likewise could not be considered as establishing proof of a crime, but rather indications of what needed to be checked out. Pavkovic's report based on the unconfirmed story of his security organs, P1440, as to Gornje Obrinje was likewise internal to the VJ and not brought to the attention of Lukic. That which Lukic did know was demonstrated by the meeting evidenced at 6D803, which talked of the rumours of a crime at Gornje Obrinje and the difficulties encountered in trying to confirm the information and conduct an investigation. From this meeting in October of 1998, we see that Lukic was informed by the state security about the Albanian press circulating sensationalised stories about Gornje Obrinje which had been characterised by the state security as false propaganda. Under the same scenario, President Milutinovic was acquitted. As the police is concerned with hard evidence and substantive investigations rather than mere rumours, it is important to look at what was established as to Gornje Obrinje. International diplomats trying to investigate, like Jan Kickert, were unable to confirm the crime had occurred. Even the judgement at paragraph 910 of book I confirms that. Kickert testified at trial of personal knowledge of the efforts to perform an on-site investigation by the Serbian investigative judge; that's in the same paragraph. We had the evidence that the investigative team could not perform the on-site investigation because of the threat of attack by the KLA on the investigative team. Witness Marinkovic at transcript page 23526 talks about that. She was the investigative judge and she confirmed that the Serbian MUP tried to secure the site to assist her investigation, but an investigation was prevented by threats from the KLA. Thus, there was no conclusion under the domestic law that a criminal homicide had occurred. Whether the deaths were due to foul play, whether the foul play was attributable to a known perpetrator, let alone whether the perpetrator was a member of the Serbian security forces, what was a professional and life-long police officer like Lukic supposed to conclude from this paucity of evidence? It should be noted that no Kosovo Verification Mission or KDOM witnesses confirmed that a crime had been established in Gornje Obrinje, not Shaun Byrnes, not Colonel Crosland, not General DZ, and not Colonel Ciaglinski. Leaving Gornje Obrinje, let us turn to other events from 1998 analysed by the Trial Chamber. The judgement analyses a total of nine anti-terrorist actions conducted jointly by the police and the VJ in 1998, inclusive of Gornje Obrinje; this is at paragraphs 848 through 912 of book I of the judgement. The Chamber in its analysis concluded that only in one out of the nine operations was there any evidence of civilians being killed, and that was Gornje Obrinje --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic is kindly asked to slow down for interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- for which the paucity of the evidence had already been discussed. This would mean that the other eight actions did not exhibit any elements that would provide notice to Lukic or anyone else of the crimes of murder that could be imputed to a JCE for deportation. The judgement found that in five out of the other eight actions there was no indicia of either crimes or excessive force occurring. Look to paragraphs 853, 860, 869, 873, and 898 of book I. Under this set of facts, it is illogical for any Chamber to conclude that murders and indeed different crimes, such as deportation and forcible transfer, would result in 1999 as part of a future JCE when anti-terrorist actions were again conducted. What could Lukic conclude from the fact that in one of nine anti-terrorist operations there were unverified rumours of civilian deaths that the authorities tried to investigate but were prevented in doing so by the KLA? Surely the existence of a widespread and systematic JCE to deport the Kosovo Albanian population is not the only reasonable conclusion available under this evidence. Since it is not the only reasonable conclusion under the evidence, any approach that automatically assumes a criminal mens rea for a future JCE from past crimes of a different nature is flawed and in error. As to your fifth question for us, relating to whether the incident at Tusilje should have been pleaded in the indictment and whether it was cured or the prejudice to the accused resulting therefrom, we would like to say as follows. The case law is clear that a Trial Chamber has erred when it enters convictions depending on material facts that were not properly pleaded in an indictment; this is paragraph 1112 [sic] of the Kupreskic appeals judgement. The judgement in our case references Tusilje in multiple paragraphs in book II and the Chamber makes several findings linking Tusilje to the same status as incidents in the indictment; see, for instance, book II, paragraph 1219. It then bases its findings that there was an attack upon the civilian population based on these findings, including Tusilje. Thus, it is clear that the convictions of the trial judgement are based on material facts that the Defence was not put on notice of in the judgement [sic]. Thus, the Trial Chamber erred, rendering the judgement unsafe. It is the position of the Defence that this defect in the indictment could not be cured and that the Defence could not be rightly put on notice that any events in Tusilje would be considered to convict the appellant. Indeed, had that been the case the appellant would have presented Defence evidence as to Tusilje, which the Defence did not, because Tusilje was not in the indictment. Your Honours, I now briefly highlight some of the main points from our appeal. At the outset I must stress that the Appeals Chamber must step in where, as is the case here, factual findings are tainted by multiple errors of law and fact. This is in line with the Kordic and Cerkez appeals judgement at paragraphs 18 through 19. Likewise, as the Appeals Chamber has reaffirmed in two recent decisions - in the Gotovina case at paragraph 93 and the Mugenzi case at paragraphs 91 and 136 - where it is not reasonable for a Trial Chamber to find that the only possible interpretation of events involved a criminal purpose and JCE, reversal and acquittal is warranted. It is submitted that the factual errors in the judgement are so many and go to the heart of the judgement that a limited review is appropriate, as no reasonable Chamber could have excluded the alternative interpretations of events possible under the evidence. And thus, Lukic should not have been convicted of participating in a JCE. Absent such a review, a miscarriage of justice would result. It is respectfully submitted that, reviewing the errors raised in our appellant's brief, it becomes clear that the Trial Chamber consistently made inferences about the existence of a JCE, Mr. Lukic's knowledge of the same, and his intent to join the same, and his voluntary joining of such a criminal purpose, when in fact alternative and reasonable conclusions were available under the evidence that demonstrate the opposite, that Lukic was trying to uphold law and order and not commit crimes. As to mens rea, it is a reasonable conclusion to reach from the evidence that Lukic was engaged in actions appropriate for a police officer, attempting to uphold law and order in a difficult situation, faced with a terrorist insurgency, NATO air strikes, and limited authority. The judgement forgets that in 1999 NATO planes were bombing all over Kosovo which cannot be ignored. In order to assess the judgement's error, it is necessary to take into account that Lukic's arrival to Kosovo, just like all his actions, was dictated by a compliance with the law and was not voluntary, let alone with intent to conduct crimes. Lukic was sent to Kosovo by force of law, which permitted a member of the MUP to be assigned by the minister to any position anywhere on the territory of Serbia. This law is in evidence at P1737, Article 72. The record demonstrates that all three decisions sending Lukic to Kosovo, P1252, P1505, and P1811, all invoke Article 72 of this law. Article 33 of the law dictates that an employee of the ministry is duty-bound to carry out the orders of the minister if they do not themselves amount to a criminal offence on their face. The text of the aforementioned decisions makes clear that what was being asked of Lukic was the regular and normal performance of police duties, not anything that could be construed as criminal acts. Further, it is significant to note that President Milutinovic who was acquitted of any role in the JCE enacted an instruction on internal affairs during the time of war, which is P993, which also in Article 7 made it mandatory for Lukic to carry out his assignments given by police superiors unless they clearly involved the commission of crime and called for disciplinary proceedings for those who refused to carry out legitimate orders. Thus, it was entirely reasonable for Lukic, like Milutinovic, to have an intent and frame of mind separate and apart from a criminal one, when performing his duties in Kosovo pursuant to orders and laws that were legitimate on their face. The Trial Chamber, in book III, paragraph 92, concedes that the problems relating to the KLA were supposed to be resolved by the state using the police and the judicial system. Thus, contrary to a finding that Lukic's acceptance of his position as head of staff involved any criminal intent, another reasonable inference under the evidence is that he was following the law and attempting to perform legal, normal police functions, in an effort to bring law and order to all citizens within his means, indeed what the Chamber had called the appropriate course of action. As part of fulfilling his duties, Lukic had to attend meetings, both in Kosovo and in Belgrade. The judgement erroneously links his attendance to Belgrade meetings as evidence that he shared in a criminal intent, a common purpose as part of a JCE. We see this in book III, paragraphs 1019, 1022, 1024, and 1040. However, this is contrary to the judgement's finding as to Milutinovic, whose presence at the same meetings was determined not to show criminal intent. We see that at book III, paragraphs 132 and 143. Further, the Appeals Chamber has recently ruled in an ICTR judgement of Mugenzi case at paragraph 139 that: "No reasonable trier of fact could have excluded the reasonable possibility that Mugenzi and Mugiraneza attended the installation ceremony for purposes other than because they shared the common criminal purpose." In that case the reasonable alternative meaning was that they attended the ceremony as a result of obligations arising from their positions as ministers. Your Honours, Lukic's attendance at meetings is also purely a result of his obligations arising from his official position, not because of any knowledge or acceptance of any criminal purpose. Instead of looking at his mere attendance at meetings, the Chamber should have focused on direct evidence of Lukic's intent as contrary to any criminal purpose. The Trial Chamber erroneously lists the criminal purpose as ensuring the continued control by Yugoslavia and Serbia over Kosovo by criminal means, to wit, the deportation of the Albanian population. This is in book III, paragraph 95. No reasonable trier of fact could exclude the possibility that continued sovereignty over Kosovo was envisioned as a legitimate and legal function of the state. Also, no evidence can demonstrate Lukic knew of any nefarious or illegal element such as the removing of Albanians. In relation to the continued sovereignty over Kosovo, this is a recognised tenet of the Constitution of Serbia, rather than any criminal goal or purpose. This tenet was reiterated and confirmed by all the international instruments drafted during the relevant time-period, including the Resolutions of the UN Security Council, P455, P456, P433; also including the Contact Group proposals discussed at paragraph 314 of book I; and the principles of the Contact Group at paragraph 354 of the same book; the Gelbard statement, that is 6D1491; the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement, that is 1D204; the Jovanovic-Cermak Agreement, that is P432; the Perisic-Clark Agreement at P454; and the Kumanovo Accords at 6D611. Under this backdrop it is illogical to see how and why Lukic had to understand such a tenet as requiring criminal purpose and criminal means to be attained when the international community itself promoted the sovereignty of Serbia and Yugoslavia over Kosovo. This past Monday the Prosecution again identified Slobodan Milosevic as playing a pivotal role in the JCE. As to the erroneous conclusion that Lukic shared the intent of Milosevic and other alleged members of the JCE to commit crimes, the Trial Chamber in book III, paragraph 1115 did not offer a single piece of evidence. Indeed, the evidence to the contrary demonstrates that Lukic stands apart from other named members of the alleged JCE. He was neither a person close to nor trusted by President Milosevic nor MUP Minister Stojiljkovic. The evidence is clear. Indeed, the Trial Chamber itself confirms at book III, paragraph 85, that Lukic did not fit the pattern of persons said to be carefully positioned to high-level positions by Milosevic. It is clear from the evidence that Lukic, rather than being promoted by Milosevic, was demoted in 1991. We can see this from P948, 6D1360, 1D680, and is also confirmed in the judgement at book III, paragraph 937. In May of 1997, Stojiljkovic, presumably with the prior consultation with Milosevic appointed a major to be the SUP chief and to be Lukic's immediate superior. It should be noted at this time Lukic was a general in rank. And we see that from the testimony of Golubovic at transcript page 7426 as well as 6D1458 and 6D1457. Even when Lukic was sent to Kosovo, the evidence is clear that two high-level assistants of Stojiljkovic were in Kosovo, Assistant Minister Obrad Stevanovic, who was also the PJP commander; and Vlastimir Djordjevic, the chief of the public security sector and deputy MUP minister. The judgement finds that Lukic's appointment did not replace the existing command structures of the MUP. This is at paragraph 1012 of book III. Further, we have evidence of another alleged close associate of Milosevic, General Ojdanic, the Chief of Staff of the VJ, for whom the judgement confirms he was carefully positioned by Milosevic to replace General Perisic who was less malleable to Milosevic's whims, at book III, paragraph 85. The transcript of a meeting, 11 April 1999, chaired by Ojdanic refers to General Lukic as an adjutant, demonstrating that Lukic was not seriously considered as a major player. This is at 3D728. Furthermore, we had a key Prosecution witness, VJ General Vasiljevic, who described Lukic's role at a meeting he claimed was of a so-called Joint Command as being the "last hole on the flute, the 13th piglet." This is at transcript page 9066. Under the totality of the foregoing, no reasonable trier of fact could determine that Lukic had any command authority or that these meetings in Pristina were a place where Lukic exercised any kind of de facto authority. After the war, Lukic was not promoted to a choice position within the MUP, but rather was appointed as head of the border police administration, which at the time was the lowly fourth department in the hierarchy. Later, you will hear about what Lukic did within that position, which is also contrary to the intent to further a JCE. Lukic was only promoted and appointed to a high-level position within the MUP within 2001, after the overthrow of Milosevic by democratic forces. We see this from Prime Minister Zivkovic's 92 ter statement, 6D1607, paragraph 4. Thus, only after Milosevic and his MUP Minister Stojiljkovic, and the assistants Djordjevic and Stevanovic were removed, was Lukic able to be promoted and made chief of public security. Later in our submission you will hear how Lukic acted while in this position. Co-operation with the ICTY and transfer of accused to the Tribunal from Serbia first occurred during Lukic's tenure, and he did many other things to investigate crimes against Albanians and others committed during the prevailing years. One has to ask, given the foregoing evidence, would it be logical for MUP officers Stojiljkovic, Djordjevic, and Stevanovic, as named participants in an alleged JCE, to include and rely upon a person who was not of their choosing, was not trusted by them, and did not owe them any favours, and, in any event, did not hold a position that had any effective control over any units? Or would it be more logical that these named members of a JCE would exclude Lukic and would effectuate the same using their own positions within the highest leadership of the MUP and did not need Lukic. I have to remind the Chamber that the evidence at trial showed that Lukic's MUP staff at all times was comprised of only eight to ten people. The testimony of Mijatovic at 22167 through 22172 confirms that. The Trial Chamber did not perform this analysis and it is in error because it was supposed to exclude any such possibility before convicting Lukic. On the other side, would it be logical for Lukic, who devoted his life to law enforcement, to abandon the same to side with persons who had degraded and demoted him? We say it defies logic. Would it be logical for Lukic to be promoted to the head of the MUP after the fall of Milosevic and would it be logical for him to initiate co-operation with the ICTY and investigation of crimes if in fact he were involved in these crimes? We say that defies logic. If we can now return to focus on the time-period of the indictment, I think it is essential to review the evidence on record that demonstrate the intent of Lukic to be contrary of any criminal enterprise as this demonstrates the further error of the Chamber. In book III, paragraph 918, the judgement rightly gave credit to Lazarevic for a limited number of efforts by way of written declaration to ensure the army acted appropriately in carrying out its duties. As to Lukic, the Trial Chamber first acknowledges that Lukic issued what it calls orders to direct the police to prevent crimes and prevent the departure of civilians from Kosovo and even likens them to these VJ orders to abide by the law which, it says, were violated by the forces. But Lukic's written reminders for the police to adhere to the law and treat civilians accordingly were viewed in a negative light by the Chamber. Look at paragraphs 1124 and 1129 of book III. These steps by Lukic, even from a position where he had a limited authority, demonstrate that he did not share any intent to commit crimes against ethnic Albanians. Rather, Lukic committed himself to call for measures to be undertaken to prevent crimes and prevent mistreatment against Albanians and for punishment of all persons found to be committing these crimes, including police members. It is submitted that 12 key pieces of evidence were erroneously analysed by the Trial Chamber and that these documents demonstrate Lukic's true intent and character. All of these exhibits are first hand from Lukic, containing either what he said or wrote. A brief overview of this evidence demonstrates that each of these 12 dispatches and reports from meetings of encouragement and reminders issued by Lukic call for energetic measures by the police to prevent any mistreatment of Kosovo Albanians, that the police prevent persons from evicting Kosovo Albanians from their homes, that measures be taken to apprehend criminals and terrorists, and that citizens should be persuaded not to leave their villages by guaranteeing that safety measures in accord with the law would be taken. These documentary exhibits are as follows: 6D768, dated 7 August 1998; 6D872, dated 23 February 1999; 6D666, dated 3 April 1999; P1989, dated 4 April 1999; 6D778, dated 15 April 1999; 6D874, dated 6 May 1999; P1996, dated 7 May 1999; 6D773, dated 8 May 1999; P1993, dated 11 May 1999; 5D1423, dated 12 May 1999; 5D1418, dated 26 May 1999; 5D1421 dated 11 June 1999; and P1468 at various dates. The Trial Chamber, at paragraph 1129 of book III, tries to cast these, what it calls, orders by Lukic as not being genuine. However, elsewhere, at paragraphs 92, 173, 1001 of book III, it relies on his same items as genuine orders demonstrating that Lukic had a command role and authority over MUP units. Respectfully, Your Honours, you can't have your cake and eat it too. Either these orders were genuine and show Lukic did not intend crimes but perhaps lacked authority to enforce his orders, or they are not genuine; and in that case cannot demonstrate any command authority for Lukic. The Trial Chamber failed to analyse or exclude the reasonable alternative, that these orders were genuine but that Lukic had no authority over MUP forces. Now I would like to return to a point we have alluded to, the limited authority of Lukic as head of the MUP staff for Kosovo. These 12 documents are important to understand why it would be impossible for Lukic to significantly contribute and further any objective of any criminal purpose on the one hand and why the Trial Chamber erred in dismissing them as not genuine. At book III, paragraph 1129, the judgement claims that Lukic, despite his knowledge of the events on the ground, nevertheless continued to order the MUP to engage in joint operations with the VJ and uses this to claim that his orders for prevention and mistreatment of civilians are not genuine. There is no supporting evidence cited that Lukic had a authority to order the MUP to continue engaging in joint operations. To the contrary, a plethora of evidence is on the record that Lukic did not have effective control or command authority. Lukic did not have authority to punish or discipline any MUP personnel directly. This is conceded by the Trial Chamber, at book III, paragraph 1049. It is thus inconceivable for Lukic to have command authority over the MUP when the judgement confirms he did not have the power to punish. Without such a power, one cannot enforce adherence to any orders. The evidence that Lukic could not institute criminal proceedings against police members includes 6D1613, paragraph 43. The evidence that Lukic was not authorised to make decisions as to instituting disciplinary proceedings against police members can be found, for instance, at 6D1613, 6D1340, and the testimony of Witness Cvetic at 8152 through 53. Further, we have the order of President Milutinovic discussed previously as to the disciplinary rules of the MUP which did not identify either the MUP staff or Lukic as having any such authority; that is P993. The evidence we have just cited demonstrates that police superiors did not have an obligation either to inform Lukic nor seek his approval for instituting disciplinary actions against their subordinate police officers. That Lukic had no role is seen also by 6D133 and 6D1342 which the republican MUP sent out delineating regulations for disciplinary proceedings during the time of war, where, again, he was not even foreseen to be informed of such instances. Another factor to consider is that Lukic did not even have authority to reassign or remove any police member, even members of his own staff; P1884 demonstrates that fact. And P1885 and P1886 demonstrate that when officers of the SUPs were replaced and new persons appointed, these decisions originated from deputy minister and chief of public security Djordjevic, not Lukic. Insofar as the Chamber did not make a difference between the period before and during the NATO bombing campaign, it further did not take into account that there was no room for Lukic to have any command type authority, since during the time of war assistant minister and commander of all the PJP, General Obrad Stevanovic, who was also the chief of the police administration, was on the ground in Kosovo for the entire duration of the war and out in the field with the PJP units. This can be seen from P948, the testimony of Mijatovic at 22255; the testimony of Vucurevic at 63064 -- 23064; Bogunovic's 92 ter statement, 6D1614, paragraphs 6, 67, and 76; the testimony of Ilic at 24418; and Zivaljevic at 24927. This error is despite the fact that the judgement recognises that Obrad Stevanovic and Vlastimir Djordjevic were the only MUP members present when the issue of resubordination of the MUP to the VJ was at issue, not Lukic. Look to book I, 1170 of the judgement for that. The evidence is also clear that Lukic did not take part in drafting the global plan for terrorism -- for suppression of terrorism. The Trial Chamber itself confirms this at paragraph 1021. Having so found, the Chamber then erred attributing to Lukic a commanding role as to this global plan, at paragraphs 985 and 1058 and 1051 of book III. All anti-terrorist actions in 1998 were carried out under the global plan and this same modus was used in 1999 as well with the military planning the actions. That Lukic did not have a role in planning anti-terrorist actions of the VJ or the police was confirmed by multiple witnesses from within the police and the VJ, but most notably by Chamber Witness Colonel Djakovic at transcript page 26536 through 538; 26522 through 23. And also Mijatovic at transcript 22197 through 8, and Adamovic at 24976 through 77. As part of the overall totality of the evidence it must be recalled that the Law on Defence, Article 16, stipulates that at the time of war the army commands all combat activities. There is simply no room for Lukic. This is P985. Lastly on this topic, I would like to highlight that the judgement erroneously attributes to Lukic an instrumental role in communications between Belgrade and Kosovo, in book III, paragraph 1059. However, this is in contradiction to other findings that actually summarise the evidence. For instance, book III, 1090, confirms that per the rules of the MUP - that would be P1044 - the seven SUPs on the territory of Kosovo have to send their dispatch reports directly to Belgrade and also to the MUP staff. It is thus more than clear from this that Lukic's staff only received reports in parallel and in no instance could have information that Belgrade did not already have from the field. On the issue of notice of crimes by the MUP and VJ, the Chamber, at book III, paragraph 1134, relies on a 6 May 1999 dispatch forwarding a news article to SUP chiefs from the MUP staff, following a meeting in Belgrade where, among others, Milosevic was present and so was Lukic. However, the article in question does not relate to any allegations of crimes committed by the MUP and neither did that Milosevic meeting. Further, the crimes in question were being rightly investigated by the appropriate authorities. This dispatch urges police to act in accord with the law and professionally to prevent persons attempting to perpetrate such crimes. Thus, the objectivity of the Trial Chamber is placed in doubt by its misapplication of this document. The Trial Chamber also tries to attribute significant meaning to the daily overviews that were sent from the MUP staff. These were only routine summaries of normal police work based on reports from the SUPs and it is important to note that they do not contain references to crimes from the indictment. Likewise, these overviews, at most, informed Lukic of investigations underway to locate perpetrators of crimes and preserve evidence which is not the light in which the judgement represents them. Thus, these overviews could only provide Lukic with the same type of information that was the basis of President Milutinovic's acquittal. Lastly, at book III, paragraph 40, the Trial Chamber says: "... the confiscation and destruction of identity documents is some of the strongest evidence in the case going to show that the events of spring 1999 in Kosovo were part of a common purpose." As to the alleged confiscation of ID documents, the Chamber's error in considering the evidence is significant. We must keep in mind that the judgement confirms that a majority of witnesses said this was done at the border - this is in book III, paragraph 32 - and by "majority of witnesses," this does not mean a majority of those that testified because, as we know, only 26 out of 62 Kosovo Albanian witnesses spoke of witnessing such confiscation and even fewer claimed to have been personally victims of such confiscation. We can see that evidence summarised in the same paragraph of the judgement. Respectfully, this is not enough to conclude a common criminal purpose, nor is it sufficient to demonstrate the strongest evidence of a common purpose, as the Chamber concludes in paragraph 40. In any event, the error as to Lukic is compounded by the fact that the Chamber conceded he did not have authority over the border police stations, where such confiscations allegedly occurred; and that is a finding from book III, paragraph 1075. Also, the evidence of record is that there are only allegations of such confiscations occurring at one of the several border crossings that were in existence, six in total. The Chamber's error as to identity documents did not adequately take into consideration that under the existing domestic law, which would be 1D226, the Law on Yugoslav citizenship, the loss of such identity documents did not in any way destroy the citizenship records of an individual. Indeed, later you will hear how Lukic undertook to issue new passports to 220.000 Kosovo Albanian citizens after the period of the indictment. I would now like to address our arguments as to mitigation, per Rule 101(B)(ii). The judgement having entered an erroneous finding of guilt improperly compounded that error by misapplying the law of mitigation. It is submitted that Lukic is entitled, at the very least, to a significant reduction in sentence. There are three factors in mitigation that apply. These factors are: First, Lukic's voluntary surrender and interview; then his assistance in an investigation and contribution to law and order in a number of cases connected to the crimes against Albanian civilians including some crimes in the indictment; and, third, is his deteriorated health and personal circumstance. At this time I would like to point out the most glaring error of the Trial Chamber that first acknowledges, in book III, paragraph 1202, that Lukic is entitled to credit for mitigating factors unique to him, but then it declines to give such credit and sentences him uniformly with other accused lacking such personal mitigation evidence. This is at book III, paragraph 1205. Your Honours, this violates the very purpose behind Rule 101(B)(ii). The trial judgement at paragraph 1152 of book III recognised that under the jurisprudence voluntary surrender and co-operation are to be afforded status as mitigation. It is submitted that the Trial Chamber erred and unfairly deprived Lukic of the benefit of his voluntary surrender and interview given to the Prosecution. While correctly acknowledging that co-accused Lazarevic was entitled to mitigation credit for his voluntary surrender, in book III, paragraph 1200, the Trial Chamber, at book III, paragraph 1204, regarded that Lukic was not entitled to credit for his voluntary surrender. The only rationale given by the Chamber was its own prior decisions on provisional release which neither take into account the totality of the evidence nor the prevailing jurisprudence. Furthermore, the first decision cited by the Chamber in support of its conclusion does not, in fact, relate to Lukic but relates to a co-accused showing that the Chamber erred in its analysis. Likewise, as to the interview given by Lazarevic, the Chamber correctly qualifies the same as significant co-operation that is afforded mitigation credit at book III, 1198. As to Sreten Lukic, who gave his interview before ever being indicted for any crimes and without any reservations, without any limitations, without representation of counsel, the Chamber, in book III, paragraph 1202, does not afford it as constituting significant co-operation nor mitigation credit. Such disparate treatment is erroneous. Your Honours, I next want to touch on the contributions of Mr. Sreten Lukic to law and order. At book III, paragraph 1205, the Trial Chamber determined that irrespective of the personal mitigating circumstances that had been established for Mr. Lukic, he had to have an identical sentence to other co-accused found to be part of the JCE.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As to Lukic, there was significant evidence that he worked within his mandate in different posts in the MUP after 1999 to contribute to peace and reconciliation and bring justice to all crime victims, including Albanians. Even though the Serbian MUP withdrew from Kosovo, Lukic after his appointment as head of the department issuing ID documents, undertook to facilitate the issuance of new ID documents to Kosovo Albanians through an office in Pristina, all until the head of that office was assassinated by the KLA. We have the testimony of Dujkovic at 23367 of the transcript on that. Then Lukic opened a satellite office to continue this work in Nis, the closest major city to Pristina. The evidence shows that most of the persons obtaining documents were ethnic Albanians. From Dujkovic, transcript page 23367 through 23368, we see that in evidence. And as I've mentioned, in this manner over 220.000 new passports were issued to Kosovo Albanians in a short time immediately after the war during Lukic's tenure in this department. We see that from Odalovic at transcript page 14447 through 14448. After the ouster of Milosevic, Lukic was appointed by the democratic authorities as chief of the public security sector and thus attained more powers. At that time, based on information from media reports, Lukic spear-headed the commencement of unfetterred and wide-scale investigations by the MUP as to mass graves and war crimes dating from the Kosovo war. We -- I would urge Your Honours to look at the record in our final trial brief at paragraphs 1464 through 1485. We summarised the evidence on that which was significant. Further, he promoted and facilitated co-operation between the MUP and the ICTY as to ongoing investigations. The final trial brief at paragraphs 1486 through 1507 summarise that, and that was before the Trial Chamber. This was all in spite of the unpopularity of such actions and threats made to his life and safety when he set up a Working Group to investigate claims of cover-ups of atrocities perpetrated against Albanians. I would point to Prosecution Witness K84 at transcript page 5228. Indeed, Defence and Prosecution witnesses talked of Lukic's integral role in post-conflict efforts to uncover crimes in Kosovo and promote justice, including co-operation with the ICTY; those would be K84, 6D2, Zivkovic, Kostic, and Furdulovic. Lukic initiated a project to gather all documentation from Kosovo, to preserve records, so as to assist in prosecutions of perpetrators even after the war. Witness Kostic talked about that at T.24104. Further, Lukic undertook to try and resolve the tensions in the south of Serbia by creating a new multi-ethnic police in that region which included Albanians. Dujkovic at transcript page 23369 and Zivkovic at transcript page 24685 talked about this. Indeed, the Trial Chamber recognised some of this and at book III, paragraph 1202, found that: "... Lukic contributed to law and order in a number of cases connected to the crimes in the indictment, and therefore we will take this into account in mitigation when determining his sentence." However, the Chamber did not follow through with its own finding. The Chamber's negation of mitigating factors is improper. It also sends the wrong signal, which would stifle efforts of others, contemplating personal sacrifice to promote law and order. If an individual who puts his life on the line to investigate crimes and bring perpetrators to justice is not afforded mitigation credit and is to be punished equally with others who do not have evidence of such efforts, then where is justice and what is the meaning of Rule 101(B)(ii)? Here Sreten Lukic personally undertook when he came to a position within the police where he could do so, to have investigations carried out on crimes, including those from this indictment, and spear-headed the first steps for co-operation between Serbia and the Tribunal. It should be noted that under the leadership of Lukic, the Serbian MUP made the first arrests and transfers of ICTY indictees, eight in total, and transferred seven more persons to the Tribunal pursuant to voluntary surrenders. I would like to now turn to the diminished health of Lukic. First of all, it is apparent from the face of the judgement that the Chamber did not review all the pertinent filings when it said on book III, paragraph 1202: "The Chamber has re-examined the relevant documentation in the record of the proceedings but does not consider that Lukic's state of health rises to the level that would warrant mitigation of his sentence." The Chamber's review was only of less serious health complications, which we see from the decisions -- from the filings cited in the footnote. These were a bad back and tooth problems, and the Chamber ignored and did not mention the very serious condition that required two cardiac surgeries before Lukic's surrender, one of which resection of an aneurism of the ascending aorta with interposed graft and replacement of the aortic valve in 2004 is regarded as one of the most serious cardiac invasive procedures. The seriousness of the Trial Chamber's error is best illustrated by the information that this Chamber now has before it. Appendix B to the appellant's brief demonstrates the underlying medical condition and the serious problems that plagued his treatment upon his arrival to the Tribunal. You now also have on the record from the provisional release filings the report of medical professionals dated 13 February 2002 [sic] and 21 January 2013 respectively, from which we see that: "The survival rate among socially isolated patients with coronary disease is twice lower than that among socially integrated patients in the short term ... studies in Sweden have shown that the ten-year survival rate of patients with coronary heart disease is three times better among socially integrated patients than isolated ones." The Appeals Chamber should rightly consider that this current 22-year sentence against Lukic is, in fact, potentially a life sentence due to the morbidity statistics set forth by the medical professionals. This should be viewed as a mitigating factor and should be taken into account. And at this time, Your Honour, I don't know whether we should have the break prematurely or if I can pass the podium to my colleague, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe we will have the break right now and we will resume at quarter to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, counsel for Mr. Lukic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. To spare you from my heavy accent, I will give this part in B/C/S so you receive proper translation. [Interpretation] First of all, a small digression. My colleague, Mr. Ivetic, mentioned, among others, two people, those are Obrad Stevanovic and Mr. Djordjevic. We should like to point out to Your Honours that both these persons throughout 1998 and 1999 were superior to Mr. Sreten Lukic. I shall now deal with only some of the errors in fact made in the trial judgement relative to our client. You have heard on this topic from other Defence teams relative to other accused in this case. Our Defence believes that the established practice in this Tribunal is that the Appeals Chamber must intervene when it is clear that the Trial Chamber has committed numerous errors in fact and in law. We would mention not only the dissenting opinion of Judge Morrison on the appeal judgement in the Milan and Sredoje Lukic case, paragraph 8, but also the appeal judgement in the Kordic and Cerkez case, paragraphs 18 and 19, as well as the judgement in the Blaskic case. In our appeal brief we have only partially outlined some of these errors because account had to be taken within the limit of words also of other grounds of appeal that this Defence deems important. Thus, the scope of the errors stated in our appeal brief does not nearly reflect the actual extent of the errors. On this occasion, we shall deal only with the errors noted in Volume III of the judgement. We emphasise that the findings and conclusions in 45 paragraphs of Volume III, which is almost one-fourth of the paragraphs related to my client, rely on erroneous, incorrect, inconsistent, and incompletely quoted 194 exhibits that were thus erroneously analysed. This fact cannot and must not be ignored. The judgement does not reflect the actual state of facts, and it is therefore evident that the Trial Chamber, due to these errors, erroneously made legal conclusions on the role of Sreten Lukic and therefore also erroneous conclusions on his liability. The massive number and the substance of these errors considerably invalidate the findings and the conclusions of the Trial Chamber. The judgement is replete with findings and conclusions referencing footnotes, but when one reads the exhibits from those footnotes they simply fail to corroborate the findings and conclusions from the paragraphs of the judgement. If the judgement were to be read on its own, it makes sense; but it does not make sense if the allegations, the findings, and conclusions of the Trial Chamber are cross-checked with the exhibits referenced in the footnotes. This has led to a great injustice done to my client because based on these and such numerous errors, erroneous legal conclusions were made on the liability of my client. We have divided these errors today into several groups. The first groups are errors related to overviews of daily events and incidents made by the MUP staff in Kosovo. These overviews were made on the basis of reports received from secretariats of internal affairs in Kosovo, and as we have heard those reports were in parallel and primarily sent to the headquarters of the MUP in Belgrade and copied to the MUP staff in Pristina for their information. Although the source documents state that they are overviews, the Trial Chamber persistently calls them reports, which makes an essential difference. Most of the reports had already been sent to the MUP staff in Belgrade. We can see that from the numbers of the documents cited in the reference numbers allocated by the staff. These documents are used by the Trial Chamber as evidence in making conclusions on various issues concerning the powers and the role of Mr. Lukic as head of that staff. As a rule, the Chamber attempts to prove the opposite of what these reports show; namely, the conclusive finding concerning these overviews is cited in para 1059, referencing footnote 2657, where the Chamber states: "Lukic's name is printed at the end of every report, but he did not sign those reports physically." Despite this conclusion, in the concluding paragraph, 1123 of Volume III, the Chamber states how these reports were made and what Lukic knew about the events in Kosovo. "They were later integrated into one comprehensive report that Lukic signed and sent to the MUP in Belgrade." The statement that Lukic signed and sent is directly opposite to the previous finding of the Chamber, where it stated that Lukic did not sign these reports. In several paragraphs the Chamber references these reports as evidence that Lukic had knowledge that he was an important chain in reporting and similar, saying that Lukic signed these reports. However, the fact is that none of these reports were signed by Lukic himself, also because those reports were not even in the possession of Sreten Lukic because it was the routine work of the analyst at the staff. The analyst was Desimir Slovic prior to the bombing, and after he was wounded in the NATO bombing of Pristina at the beginning of the conflict he was replaced by Vojislav Gucic. The reports that Sreten Lukic saw could only inform him that criminal acts were being detected and duly prosecuted, and the same applies to all the reports that are not even all part of the case file, although we have given them all to the OTP, and in this case we have 30 such reports in evidence. Each of these reports states that crimes were being detected and duly prosecuted. The judgement, however, relies on its own erroneous interpretation of reports in a large number of paragraphs: Volume III, 1052 [sic], 48 reports in the footnote 2639, 26 reports in footnote 2640, 22 reports in footnote 2641; Volume III, 1054, four reports in footnotes from 2654 to 2648; then Volume III, 1090, quotes 6D1246; Volume III, 1091, references 6D1239 on three occasions; Volume III, 1094, 6D1242, P1693; Volume III, 1096, 16 report stated in footnote 2751; Volume III, 1123, eight reports in footnote 2824; Volume III, 1124, 16 reports in footnote 2826. From this we see that in eight paragraphs 146 reports are referenced which the Trial Chamber says have been signed by Lukic which is not confirmed by any of the reports themselves. Precisely this massive number creates a false impression of the role and powers of Sreten Lukic and his knowledge of crimes. One should emphasise that the case file contains a total of 30 overviews of the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija, but their repetitive references to them create the false impression that they are much more numerous. Another group of errors concerned the conclusions of the Chamber when it says that Lukic issued an order, an instruction, or similar and signed them personally which is refuted by the source documents invoked by the Chamber. None of these documents were physically signed by Lukic. They were signed instead by members of the staff and even some generals from Belgrade who came to Kosovo and used the premises of the staff and even the letter-head of the staff and its leader. With Exhibit 6D874 referenced in footnote 2528 and with paragraph 1005, Volume III, the Chamber states the following: "The Chamber notes that even if the dispatch was not sent by Lukic, it was nevertheless sent from the MUP staff in his name. No suggestion was made that it was unauthorised." In contrast to this, we have the testimony of Gvozden Gagic who explained the entire process of the drafting and sending of this document, stating clearly that Sreten Lukic not only did not participate in writing this document, but that he was not even informed of its sending from the address of the staff, nor was any authorisation sought from him. It was explained also that a different person signed the document, although at the bottom of the document we find the name of Sreten Lukic. This is the testimony of Gvozden Gagic, T.24476/24 to T.24478/13. Therefore, no decision or approval was needed from Sreten Lukic to send something from the MUP staff. That was also the only address from which his superior, Obrad Stevanovic, wrote and sent documents whenever he was in Pristina instead of in the field with PJP units. We find similar erroneous conclusions of the Chamber also in the following paragraphs and exhibits: Volume III, para 988, Exhibit 6D690 and P2528; paragraph 1004, Volume III, Exhibit 6D237; Volume III, paragraph 1005, Exhibit 5D1289; Volume III, 1093, Exhibit 6D874; Volume III, para 1092, Exhibit 6D874 and 6D876; Volume III, para 1095, Exhibit 5D1289. In these six paragraphs the Chamber derives erroneous conclusions related to nine exhibits. The next group of conclusions involving inaccurate, incomplete, or inconsistent citation or interpretation of exhibits. Again, due to the massive number of these errors, the Chamber made erroneous findings and ultimately erroneous conclusions, and as a rule these findings and conclusions went to the detriment of Lukic. Therefore, had the Trial Chamber used correct and accurate interpretations of the said evidence, it would have reasonably reached different conclusions that would be in favour of Lukic's Defence. We're going to give you a flagrant example from Volume III, 1031, where the Chamber cites that Lukic mentioned that there are allegedly -- there is an alleged mass grave in the section of Jablanica and cites P1468, page 134. In the next paragraph, Volume III, 1032, it says that this example indicates that Lukic was informed about the activities of the MUP which would indicate that the mentioned mass grave was the result of action by the state forces. The exhibits to which the Chamber refers do not indicate anything like that. Quite to the contrary. Numerous exhibits show that Jablanica was in territory under the control of the KLA and that the KLA staff was also located in Jablanica at the time. Thus, Lukic is referring to crimes of the KLA, and we can see that from Exhibits 5D1307, 4D137, 4D140. Brahimaj was even convicted before this Tribunal for some crimes committed in Jablanica. Then we have paragraph 1056, where the Trial Chamber states that in the report by the staff, 6D1239, the case of finding bodies of unidentified civilians were found which is completely contrary to the original exhibit, where it states that in the area of action by Siptar terrorist forces unidentified bodies of men were found and that the investigating judge was informed about it. So the Chamber omitted the main indicator, the area of action by the Siptar terrorist forces which qualifies Lukic's knowledge as to the bodies being of casualties of battle. Furthermore, this qualifier, unidentified men, is changed, and it says that these were bodies of civilians. In Volume III, paragraph 1054, the Chamber states that in 6D808 says that records were being maintained about the number of Albanians leaving Kosovo. The Trial Chamber thereby wishes to show that this notification was, in essence, discriminatory in relation to Albanians -- actually, quite to the contrary. If you read the document you can see that it is seeking various data. Among other things, it requests information about persons of Albanian and other ethnic communities who have fled from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic, I believe that the time allocated to your submission is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If that is so, then I just need one minute to thank Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Due to all of the above stated in our appeal and in response of the appeal by the Prosecutor as well as all that we said today in our oral submissions, we would ask the Appeals Chamber to issue an acquittal of our client. We would like to thank the Chamber for listening to us, for taking into account our reasons and for reviewing them, and we hope that you would correct the errors that we pointed to and that you would hand down an acquittal on the basis of our submissions today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one thing I would like to seek some clarification from you, that is on page 47, line 5, you are talking about a case of the identified bodies of the civilians. Well, I wonder whether that is the case concerning the 287 individuals who were murdered in Djakovica municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, maybe I mispronounced, it's Jablanica, not Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judge T has a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I already sat down. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: You can stand up any time or sit down any time. I would like to refer you to your brief rather to something -- with -- part of your brief which was left out of the oral presentation today, and this is the part where you refer to documents underlying Exhibit 6D614 and the brief claims that those documents were of critical nature. And if you could explain what exactly those documents were. Are you with me, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, but I think that my co-counsel will answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: I think so. I think that's more appropriate for him to answer because this refers to his portion of the presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: So I would like to know what exactly those documents were, and why, in your opinion, are they so critical to your defence? And you also claim in your brief that by not admitting, by denying those documents, the Trial Chamber made an error. So if you could also elaborate on that error that allegedly in your opinion was committed by the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will gladly address that and I thank you for your question. 6D614 was a compendium. It was part of this dossier of documents that Sreten Lukic as head of the MUP after the war asked for all the documents to be collected, evidencing crimes that occurred and evidencing all the evidence that the authorities had collected to assist in prosecutions. 6D614 categorises the documentation and demonstrates that the crimes that were being committed were being investigated by the authorities and were being then prepared for prosecution, and it shows that during the time-period of the NATO bombing of Kosovo, the Serbian MUP, in fact, did investigate, did name and apprehend members of the police, members of the army, and members of the -- regular citizens who had committed crimes, including crimes against Albanians.
