The underlying documents -- 6D614 was a summary. The underlying documents would be the original base documents collected from all the various secretariats of the interior on the territory of Kosovo as part of this project that was spear-headed by our client. And it shows, first of all, that with regards to the notice requirements, the notice that would be available to our client was that the authorities, the MUP, were doing their job, they were policing, they were investigating crimes irrespective of who the victims were, irrespective of who the alleged perpetrators were, and were doing their best to collect evidence to assist in the prosecution of these individuals. The -- we had witnesses who testified as to the creation of 6D614, and as to the base of materials that were used, the Trial Chamber only permitted us to include references from 6D614 where witnesses we brought had personal knowledge about specific items in the summary rather than allowing us to present documentary evidence that would show the entirety of the situation, which we believe would have shown a different picture. And again, with the limitation imposed on the number of hours and number of witnesses we could bring, we could not bring witnesses who had personal knowledge of each and every single incident that was investigated in Kosovo during the time-period of the NATO bombings. And I think that is the critical point of the error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see no more questions from the Bench. And thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Now we would like to hear the response from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour and good morning or good afternoon. General Lukic was an important member of the JCE. As head of the MUP staff he commanded MUP forces which committed crimes on a massive scale in Kosovo in 1999. He planned and co-ordinated the engagement of MUP forces in joint operations with the VJ throughout the province, which resulted in the crimes charged in this case. Based on this and other evidence, the Chamber correctly found that Lukic made a significant contribution to the JCE and that he shared the intent of his fellow JCE members, Pavkovic and Sainovic. In our submissions this morning, my colleague, Mr. Wood, and I will be addressing Your Honours' questions regarding the actus reus and mens rea requirement for JCE liability. I will be dealing with your question ten and specifically with the actus reus requirement for JCE I and I will also be addressing Your Honours' question regarding Lukic's involvement in the disarming process. My colleague, Mr. Wood, will be addressing Your Honours' questions regarding the mens rea requirement for JCE I and III as these relate to Lukic. And we will be dealing with some of the issues raised today by my colleagues from the Defence in relation to these questions. For all other matters that have been raised, we rest on our written submissions. But before I turn to addressing our response to Your Honours' question, a brief comment on the standard of review and Lukic's appeal. It is our position, Your Honour, that Lukic has not assisted the appeal process by his appeal brief, by his reply brief, or by his submissions here today. As we have indicated in more detail in our response brief, many of the issues he raises are, in fact, arguments he raised at trial which the Chamber expressly considered and rejected in its judgement. In doing so, he fails to show that the Chamber erred. Lukic merely picks and chooses his way through the evidence, but ignores the totality of the evidence that was considered by the Trial Chamber. He also highlights irrelevant findings in isolation, and I will return to this point later in my submissions. In addition, Lukic misinterprets the judgement and he has done so in his appeal brief and also this morning in submissions. One example is the reference we heard this morning from my colleagues to paragraph 1049 of Volume III of the judgement. The Lukic team suggested that in this paragraph the Chamber concluded that Lukic had no disciplinary powers against members of the MUP. In fact, that's not what the relevant paragraph, paragraph 1049, says. What the Chamber found, in fact, was that instructions given by Lukic in August of 1998 and February 1999 indicate that he had de facto authority to require the chiefs of the SUPs, or secretariats of internal affairs, to conduct investigation into crimes, even if he was not the one who actually initiated proceedings. So that is a very different finding than what has been indicated by my colleagues this morning. Lukic's appeal brief illustrates a misunderstanding of the Tribunal's standard of review. It also reveals a misunderstanding of the Trial Chamber's findings and judgement. This is not a case of a failure to deal with evidence, as Lukic suggests. In this case, not only did the Chamber consider the evidence carefully, but it also considered the submissions made by Lukic at trial carefully, provided reasoned opinions on its findings, and supported its conclusions with a summary discussion of the evidence. Lukic fails to show that the Chamber's findings he disagrees with or which he claims are untrue were unreasonable. His appeal simply does not meet the standard of review and should be dismissed in its entirety. I turn now to Your Honours' question number ten, and I will read it out for the record: "Discuss, as a legal matter, as well as with respect to the particular Trial Chamber's findings for each appellant convicted for JCE I, whether the actus reus and mens rea of a JCE member may be fulfilled prior to the existence of the common purpose ..." Your Honours already heard on Monday submissions from my colleague, Ms. Martin Salgado, in relation to our position on the legal matter, and I note that I will only be addressing the actus reus component of this question, as my colleague will be addressing the mens rea component. On the facts, we understand the Appeals Chamber to be asking whether Lukic was found to have contributed to the JCE prior to the existence of the common purpose. The answer to this question is no. Lukic's contribution is grounded on conduct that occurred during the period in which the crimes were committed. As head of the MUP staff, Lukic made a significant contribution to the JCE by planning, organising, and controlling MUP units and by co-ordinating joint actions with the VJ throughout the period in which the crimes were committed. In the months preceding the 1999 campaign with which this case is concerned, Lukic began to make preparations which laid the groundwork for the implementation of the common purpose. This preparatory work, included the arming of the non-Albanian population and the disarming of the Albanian population. This conduct also forms part of his contribution to the JCE, as it was carried out for the purpose of implementing the criminal plan. I intend to elaborate on this answer by explaining how Lukic contributed to the JCE and why his contribution was significant, and I will deal with two issues: First, Lukic's role as head of the MUP staff; and second, his contribution during the period when the crimes were committed, and in doing so I will address Your Honours' question regarding his involvement in the disarming process. Turning first to Lukic's role as head of the MUP staff. The Chamber found that Lukic held this position from mid-June 1998 to June 1999; this is Volume III, paragraphs 945 through 1050. The MUP staff was the entity in charge of planning, organising, controlling and directing the work of MUP forces in Kosovo, Volume III, paragraph 1012. It was based in Pristina. The Chamber correctly found that as head of the MUP staff, Lukic was the de jure and de facto commander of MUP forces deployed in Kosovo, including those units involved in combat activities; this is Volume III, paragraph 1131. In this capacity Lukic was directly involved in the planning process and he was also the person responsible for the use and engagement of MUP forces in the province, Volume III, paragraphs 1118 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Excuse me, it seems that we have a technical problem. Judge Ramaroson has no translation. Is that soft? Everything's okay. Yes. I'm sorry about that. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour, I'll continue. I was referring to Lukic's role as head of the MUP staff. And I mentioned that in this capacity he was directly involved in the planning process and he was also the person responsible for the use and engagement of MUP forces in the province; and this is Volume III, paragraph 1051, 1118 and 1131. He was also the person responsible for ensuring that the day-to-day operations of MUP forces in Kosovo were conducted in accordance with the overall plans and policies set by the MUP leadership in Belgrade and by Milosevic, Volume III, paragraph 1131. And he co-ordinated and planned joint operations with the VJ, in particular with his counterpart in the VJ, General Pavkovic, which took place from March 1999 onwards, Volume III, paragraph 1118 and 1132. If I can respond briefly to my colleagues' submissions this morning regarding the Chamber's findings on Lukic's role and authority. From having heard their submissions today, what is apparent is that nothing has changed. At trial Lukic argued that he was a general in the police with no authority over MUP units in Kosovo and that he was the head of a weak body called the MUP staff. However, the Chamber's findings that I have just outlined are based on a careful assessment of the evidence on the role and authority of the MUP staff which can be found at paragraphs 947 and -- through 1051 of Volume III. One of the pieces of evidence the Chamber considered was Lukic's own explanation of his role and responsibilities. He was, in fact, the person best placed to explain the role of the MUP staff, and in Volume III, paragraph 1013, the Chamber referred to his explanation in his interview with Prosecution officials in which he explained that the role of the MUP staff was to co-ordinate, plan, and direct MUP organisational units primarily in the task of curbing terrorism. In that same paragraph the Chamber also referred to Lukic's role vis-a-vis special police units, which are referred to as PJPs in the judgement, and it noted that Lukic himself said that these units had dual responsibility towards Obrad Stevanovic and also responded to the MUP staff. In addition, the Chamber noted that in promoting or recommending Lukic for promotion, MUP Minister Stojiljkovic commended him for his command -- successful command and control of MUP units engaged in the prevention of terrorism in Kosovo, and MUP Minister Stojiljkovic clearly knew and had a clear impression of what were the roles and responsibilities of General Lukic in Kosovo. By challenging the Trial Chamber's findings on his role and authority on appeal, Lukic merely repeats his trial submissions without showing how the Chamber erred. His challenges on this point should be rejected. I turn now to Lukic's contribution to the JCE and I will deal first with his involvement in the planning and co-ordination of MUP operations and then turn to his role in the arming and disarming process. Lukic was actively involved in the planning and co-ordination of MUP operations during the 1999 campaign, paragraphs 1131 and 1132 of Volume III. The Chamber found that the NATO bombing provided JCE members with an opportunity - for which they had been waiting and preparing - to carry out the common plan, Volume III, paragraph 92. That the MUP was preparing for a large-scale offensive in the spring of 1999 is evidenced by discussions at the MUP staff on 17th February 1999, and this meeting at the MUP staff is discussed in Volume III, paragraph 996. On that date, Lukic chaired a meeting which was attended by the highest MUP leadership from Belgrade, MUP Minister Stojiljkovic, the heads of both branches of the MUP, Vlastimir Djordjevic and Radomir Markovic as well as by assistant minister Obrad Stevanovic and by MUP commanders in Kosovo. And if we could have slide one up on the screen. Up on the screen we have the minutes of this meeting which are discussed in Volume III, paragraph 996, and we see - and these are words of Lukic that are highlighted at the top of the page - we see that Lukic sets out the situation in Kosovo and he reports on plans of the MUP staff to carry out three mopping-up operations in the areas which are described in the slide and he also refers to the personnel that has been allotted for these operations. In addition, he reports that a meeting of the MUP staff will be held in the coming days with all commanders of police unit detachments for further consultation about their engagement. And if we could have slide two up on the screen. At this same meeting MUP Minister Stojiljkovic addressed those present, and in his conclusions referring to an eventual attack by NATO he said: "Within two or three days of an attack, we have to put our plans in motion and use the time to clear the territory from terrorists." And the minutes of this meeting are Exhibit P1990 and these comments are on page 3, and he continued by setting out the forthcoming tasks as we see on the slide at the bottom. We can remove the slide. The Chamber found that the areas identified by Lukic at the 17th February 1999 meeting for these actions were the same ones envisaged by Lazarevic's Grom 3 order of 16th February 1999, confirming joint planning and co-ordination between the VJ and MUP leadership; and this is Volume I, paragraphs 1015 and 1039. The large-scale plans which the VJ and the MUP prepared in February 1999 were implemented down both chains of command in late March 1999 through a series of Joint Command orders, Volume I, paragraph 1017. During the implementation of these operations, Lukic worked closely with Joint Command members Pavkovic and Sainovic in co-ordinating the actions of the MUP and the VJ, Volume III, paragraphs 1118 and 1132. These joint MUP and VJ operations could not have taken place without the direct involvement of Lukic, head of the MUP staff. Using the MUP staff, Lukic implemented the decisions and tasks of the Joint Command involving MUP units down the MUP chain of command, and this is Volume I, paragraphs 1033 through 1042; and Volume III, paragraphs 973 to 975 and 1132. Lukic's role was to ensure the participation of MUP units in joint operations, Volume III, paragraph 1118 and 1132. This is why the Chamber found Lukic to be an important member of the JCE, Volume III, paragraph 1131. As Mr. Kremer explained on Monday, the joint MUP and VJ operations which took place from late March onwards resulted in a campaign of terror and violence against the Kosovo Albanian population. Throughout the duration of this campaign, Lukic was on the ground in Pristina and this allowed him to monitor MUP activities closely, and for reference, Your Honours, Volume III, paragraphs 999 to 1001, 1004, 1006, 1009 and 1010, and paragraph 1040. Lukic's constant presence on the ground also made him aware of the ill-treatment and the forcible displacement of scores of civilians by Serb forces, Volume III, paragraph 1124. The MUP and VJ operations continued into April and May 1999. Lukic's interventions at MUP staff meetings and his instructions to MUP commanders during this period demonstrate that he actively supervised these operations, and for the detail I refer Your Honours to Volume III, paragraphs 999 to 1011. Together with VJ forces, MUP units, which Lukic commanded, executed the JCE's plan with brutal efficiency, displacing over 700.000 Kosovo Albanian civilians in a span of two months. VJ and MUP units acted with a high degree of co-ordination in expelling the Kosovo Albanian population, and this is in Volume I, paragraphs 1033 to 1043. Despite his knowledge of the systematic nature of the crimes, Lukic continued to engage MUP units in joint operations with the VJ during the 1999 campaign, clearly intending for these crimes to take place, Volume III, paragraph 1129. I turn now to Lukic's role in the arming of non-Albanian civilians. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that you are talking about arming and disarming together. When you discuss Mr. Lukic's involvement in disarming, would you please point out the specific paragraph in the judgement as well as the specific evidence admitted during the trial related to this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I intend to do that. So turning first to Lukic's role in the arming process and I will later deal with the disarming well. Months in advance of the 1999 campaign, Lukic armed, trained, and organised non-Albanian civilians. Lukic then used armed locals during the attacks that took place from March 1999 onwards. As my colleague Mr. Menon explained on Tuesday, between July 1998 and March 1999, the non-Albanian population in Kosovo was armed and organised into so-called RPOs, or local defence units; this is Volume I, paragraph 787. The Chamber found that these units were under the general command and control of the MUP and of Lukic, Volume I, paragraph 777; and Volume III, paragraph 1067. And Lukic's involvement in the arming process throughout this period is discussed in Volume III, paragraphs 1061 through 1067. Now my colleagues this morning have referred to the arming process and have characterised it as a legal distribution of weapons and they've characterised the disarming as a voluntary surrender of illegal weapons. The Chamber, in fact, considered the legality of the arming process, but it noted that the primary issue in relation to both the arming and the disarming was the fact that it was carried out upon ethnic lines and the Chamber's findings were -- that sum up its analysis are in Volume III, paragraph 72. And what does this mean that it was carried out on ethnic lines? The Chamber found that weapons were distributed to only one ethnic group, these are non-Albanians, primarily Serbs; and that the majority of the Serb population was provided with weapons. It also found that the disarming only targeted ethnic Albanians and that the majority of the non-Albanian [sic] population was not part of the KLA. An additional factor the Chamber considered was the secrecy of the process, and my colleague this morning has characterised the arming as a public process that was -- that everyone was aware of. In paragraph 65 of Volume III, the Chamber pointed to some comments made by Lukic himself in relation to the arming process and these are comments made at a 2 November 1998 meeting. At this meeting, Lukic directed SUP chiefs and MUP commanders to conceal the fact that the Serb population had been armed from KVM verifiers. And, in addition, he instructed those present that armed Serbs were to be directed to deny that Serbs were armed in the villages if asked by KVM members and to use the excuse that only members of village guards were armed. Clearly, by making these remarks, Lukic himself did not consider the fact that the armed population had been armed as a public process, as the Lukic Defence suggests. At the 17th February meeting which I've discussed when preparations were made for a large-scale offensive, Lukic reported that members of the staff had held meetings with all RPOs and that RPOs in nearly all villages inhabited by Serbs were active and this is P1990, page 1, and it's the same exhibit that we saw earlier on a slide. When the 1999 campaign commenced, Lukic used armed locals in operations. His interventions at MUP staff meetings in April and May 1999 confirm the involvement of RPOs in these operations, Volume III, paragraph 1066. And as Your Honours have heard from my colleagues earlier this week, in Volume II of its judgement, the Chamber found that in some municipalities armed locals did, in fact, take part in actions with the MUP and the VJ aimed at expelling Kosovo Albanian civilians from their homes, Volume III [sic], paragraph 48, 432, 888, and 944. I turn now to the disarming of the ethnic Albanian population and at the break I distributed a table and I ask that it be provided to the Bench. And while that is being done, just a correction for the record, the references I just gave regarding volume -- it should state "Volume II" instead of "Volume III." I note that at line 14 of page 62 the transcript incorrectly notes "Volume III," and it's probably because I misspoke. Turning to the disarming of ethnic Albanians, just as he had been involved in the arming process, Lukic also participated in disarming the Kosovo Albanian population, and this finding is at Volume III, paragraph 1121. By disarming ethnic Albanians in the months preceding the 1999 campaign, Lukic rendered them defenceless to the Serb attacks that took place from late March 1999 onwards. Now, Your Honours have asked a question regarding Lukic's involvement in the disarming process and before I address it I will just read it out for the record. The question is: "Discuss evidence on the record, if any, showing Lukic's involvement in the disarming of the Kosovo Albanian population." The Chamber's finding that Lukic participated in the disarming process is supported by Joint Command documents on the record. These documents show that MUP units under Lukic's command carried out the disarming in 1998 and that he monitored this process closely. Now, Your Honours have been handed a table of exhibits relating to Lukic's involvement in the disarming process and I ask you to turn to this table. It has several categories of exhibits and I plan to deal with them briefly. The first category of exhibits on this table are 11 excerpts from P1468, which are the notes of meetings of the Joint Command and these are all contained on page 1 of the table. And contrary to my submission of the Defence -- to the submissions of the Defence, these excerpts show that in the period between August and October 1998, Lukic provided regular updates of the disarming of ethnic Albanian villages being carried out by MUP units. And if I can take Your Honours to one of these excerpts as an example and this is the one dated 10th September 1998, and it's towards the middle of the page. And the relevant reference is P1468, page 100. I note that this excerpt is referred to in Volume III, paragraph 1029. We can see from the relevant excerpt on this table that Lukic reports about the disarming of six ethnic Albanian villages, and he notes: "But it's not enough and it continues tomorrow ..." I should note for clarity, Your Honours, that in paragraph 1029 this meeting of -- that Lukic -- at which Lukic is reporting this information is incorrectly dated as 1st September 1998 and it should be 10th September. I will not deal with the remaining excerpts from P1468, but I will read all the relevant page numbers out for the record. And the relevant references from this exhibit are: P1468, pages 48, 49, 52, 77, 92, 97, 100, 106, 110, 131, and 139. Turning to the second category of documents on this table, these are Joint Command operative reports from the period of October and November 1998, and these are listed on both sides of the table that has been provided to Your Honours. These reports show that MUP units were actively engaged in disarming ethnic Albanian villages and that this disarming process was to continue. And if I can take Your Honours to one example and this is the second one from the bottom of page 1, and it's the reference -- exhibit reference is P1203, and it's dated 15th October 1998. And this document is referred to in Volume III, paragraph 58 of the judgement. We see here in the excerpt on the table that under the heading number III (b) engagement of MUP units, the -- IV refers to the fact that MUP units are collecting weapons from Siptar or ethnic Albanian villages which have shown a willingness to surrender them. And under the heading IV, proposal for further engagements of the MUP, the report notes that this collection of weapons will continue. I won't refer to all the different Joint Command operational reports on this table, but I will read them -- the relevant exhibit numbers and page numbers out for the record. The relevant references are P1203, pages 5 and 8; P1206, pages 4 and 7; P1204, pages 5 and 7; P1197, pages 3 and 6; and P1198, pages 4 and 6. The last exhibit on this table that I want to refer to is on page 2, and if I can ask Your Honours to turn to that, this is P2166, and it's an exhibit dated 29th October 1998. And in this exhibit is a record of a meeting that took place in Belgrade on that date and it's referred to in the Trial Chamber's judgement Volume I, paragraph 997, and it's also referred to in Volume I, paragraphs 1097 to 1195. Now, this meeting was attended, as the minutes show, by the highest Serb political military and police leadership. All three JCE members in this case were in attendance. And the excerpt we have on the table is a report that is provided by General Pavkovic at this meeting, where he presented an overview of the plan for the suppression of terrorism which was implemented in the summer of 1998. And as we can see from this excerpt, one of the tasks that General Pavkovic notes formed part of this plan was number 7, disarming all Siptar or Albanian villages which are known to be armed. If I can state -- continue discussing this meeting but ask that we turn to the next slide. What we have on the screen is a copy of the same exhibit, P2166, and this is a continuation of Pavkovic's comments -- remarks at that meeting. And on pages 4 and 5 he provides a more detailed overview of the implementation of the plan. On page 5 - and this is the portion that's been highlighted - he -- under number 8 he refers to the weapons collected and the localities from where these weapons have been collected. And if I can draw Your Honours' attention to the portion that appears in red on the screen and I'll read the quote. It says: "Sixty-six villages still need to be disarmed and some 4.000 to 5.000 guns will be seized. The villages did not take part in the terrorist operations." Now, my colleagues today have suggested that the disarming process mainly targeted KLA villages and that it was voluntary; however, what these remarks show is that villages which did not take part in terrorist operations were also disarmed by the MUP. In response to Your Honours' question on Lukic's involvement in the disarming, these are the relevant references on the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: To conclude and returning to question number 10, having planned and co-ordinated MUP operations, including joint operations with the VJ, which led to the commissions of the crimes charged, Lukic made a significant contribution to the JCE. Moreover, his contribution is grounded on conduct that occurred during the period in which the crimes were perpetrated. It is clear from the evidence I've discussed that Lukic was also actively involved in preparing for the implementation of the criminal plan and that the preparatory work he engaged in furthered the common purpose. For the reasons I've outlined, the Defence's challenges to the Chamber's findings on Lukic's contribution to the JCE should therefore be dismissed. Those are our submissions, Your Honours, in relation to the two questions that I was addressing, the actus reus question and also the disarming -- question dealing with Lukic's involvement in the disarming process. Unless Your Honours have questions for me, I will yield the floor to my colleague, Mr. Wood -- oh, we're having a break, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge T has a question to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz, counsel, I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I can't see you behind the pillar but I'll move over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: It is a very important pillar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It is. It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: You referred to in your presentation -- I should have asked this earlier but I just didn't want to interrupt you. You referred in your presentation - as did your colleagues on your side of the aisle during the course of this week - to the displacement of over 700.000 Kosovo Albanians through a campaign of terror and violence. Could you identify where in the trial judgement the Chamber found that this displacement was entirely attributable to that campaign. To put it differently, did the Trial Chamber specifically exclude the possibility that other factors during the war may have contributed to the displacement of at least a portion of those over 700.000 humans? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, the Chamber conducted a very thorough analysis of the -- of what the evidence of what happened on the ground, and this is contained in Volume II of the judgement. And it is based on that analysis of the crimes that happened and the reasons that were provided by the persons in the different localities that were expelled by Serb forces that it reached its findings which were referred to earlier this week by my colleague, Mr. Kremer, on the pattern of crimes. And the Chamber noted, when it was dealing with the pattern of crimes, that none of the witnesses who testified who came from 13 different municipalities in Kosovo and from all sorts of walks of life, none of them indicated that they had left because of the NATO bombing or because they were forced by the KLA. They clearly noted that they had been forcibly expelled from their homes by MUP and VJ forces and other forces acting together with these forces. So the Chamber's finding that this was the reason for the displacement is based on this analysis of the evidence. And the Chamber did consider whether NATO was the cause of the displacement or whether the KLA campaign was the cause of the displacement, but except for two localities where the Chamber did find that KLA members had told villagers to flee before Serb forces arrived, in the remaining of the localities this was not the reason why the population left en masse and headed towards the border. I don't know if that answers Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Yes, as posed it does. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we still have less than four minutes to go in the morning sitting, so I'm in your hands whether you would like to continue your response for the last four minutes or we'll resume in this afternoon's session, and in this way I can assure you that I'll make up for the time you lost for this morning's session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, my suggestion would be to break at this time, and that way my colleague, Mr. Wood, can just go through his submissions without any interruptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's a wise choice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We are adjourned until 2.30 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.56 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Wood, you may continue the response of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As Ms. Kravetz told you this morning, I'll be dealing with Your Honours' questions with regard to General Lukic's mens rea. That means with regard to the questions I'll be answering Your Honours' eighth and 11th questions and the mens rea component of the tenth question. I'll also address a few smaller points today raised by counsel for General Lukic and their remarks. Now, before I start, though, Your Honours I'd like to provide some citations in support of Ms. Kravetz' response to the last question before the break to show that the Chamber found that the campaign of terror and violence resulted in the forcible displacement of 700.000 Kosovo Albanian civilians. And for the record those are Volume II, paragraphs 1150 and 1175 to 78 [sic]; and Volume III, paragraphs 45, 95, and 1173. So turning to the questions then, starting with the tenth question, and I think Mr. Ivetic may have referred to that as the third question. Just for the sake of the record, Your Honour, that's the one I'll be addressing. Now, I note that you've heard this question answered twice now by Prosecution counsel, Your Honours, first by Ms. Martin Salgado and by Ms. Monchy on Monday and by Mr. Schneider on Tuesday. It won't surprise you to hear that my answer today is the same. Though the mens rea of a JCE member cannot be fulfilled prior to the existence of the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise, it can be inferred from his knowledge of crimes committed before the joint criminal enterprise came into existence. As Ms. Martin Salgado explained and contrary to counsel's remarks this morning, support for this as a matter of law can be found in the Krajisnik appeal judgement at paragraphs 200 to 204 and the Krajisnik trial judgement at paragraphs 925 and 929. So what does this mean for General Lukic's case? As the Chamber properly found, General Lukic's JCE intent is clear from his knowledge of crimes and continuing participation in the campaign of terror and violence starting in March 1999 and it can be properly inferred from his detailed knowledge of crimes committed by his MUP subordinates in 1998 and by other evidence. Now, I'll elaborate that -- on that more, Your Honours, in answering the 11th question which I think was referred to by my colleague across the aisle as the fourth question. And for the record since this is the first time this has been dealt with by the Prosecution today I'll read that question into the record, that is: "Discuss whether and under what circumstances the mens rea under JCE I for deportation and other inhumane acts (forcible transfer) may be inferred from the accused's knowledge of crimes committed in 1998, including crimes other than deportation and other inhumane acts." Now, again, Your Honours, as Ms. Martin Salgado has explained on Monday, the Chamber can draw such an inference. And under the circumstances of General Lukic's case, this is the only reasonable conclusion on the totality of the evidence from both 1998 and 1999 as the Trial Chamber properly found in paragraphs 1117 through 1130 of Volume III of the trial judgement. In short, Your Honours, because General Lukic was aware that various crimes arising from joint MUP-VJ operations resulted in massive displacements in 1998, he knew that he could use the same types of operations, using the same troops targeting the same ethnic group to achieve the same result in 1999. The fact that he continued to work to ensure the co-operation of the joint MUP-VJ operations throughout 1999 leads to the reasonable inference that he intended the massive forcible displacements starting on 24 March 1999. So what did General Lukic know in 1998? Like my colleagues who argued the Pavkovic and Lazarevic's responses, I've created a table to summarise this evidence for Your Honours' reference, and I think that's been distributed or is about to be. And again, as with my colleagues who argued the responses for Pavkovic and Lazarevic, this is for Your Honours' reference. I'll refer to only a few of those during my remarks today. The Chamber found that General Lukic knew that there were serious allegations of criminal activity by MUP forces in Kosovo directed against the Kosovo Albanian population. Now, that's the Chamber's finding at Volume III, paragraph 1086. He knew that these crimes - and these crimes included arson, murder, and forcible displacement - arose out of joint MUP-VJ operations that he helped to co-ordinate, that's Volume III, paragraphs 1012 and 1080 through 1084. For example, acts of arson were regularly discussed at Joint Command meetings that Lukic attended, including on 7 and 12 August 1998, and I refer Your Honours to Volume III, para 1080 for that finding. Further, Lukic was also informed by members of the international community about instances of arson and other crimes. For example, international monitor Shaun Byrnes told Lukic that in August and September 1998 his team observed on an almost daily basis police units burning villages, destroying crops, killing farm animals, intimidating Kosovo Albanian citizens, and driving them from their homes; that's Volume III, paragraph 1082. Now, Lukic also learned in September 1998 of the murders committed in the area of Donje and Gornje Obrinje, and that they resulted from joint MUP-VJ operations, that Lukic, as head of the MUP staff, was helping to co-ordinate and plan; that's Volume III, 1021, 1081. Now specifically, Your Honours, this incident was discussed at a Joint Command meeting that Lukic attended on 4 October 1998; that's at Volume III, para 1081. Also as my colleague across the aisle mentioned this morning in his remarks, Human Rights Watch published a detailed report about this incident. He is right it came out in 1999, it came out in February 1999, that is before the crimes in the indictment and during the same month the MUP was involved in planning the campaign, as Ms. Kravetz has explained this morning. This report was distributed to the MUP as well as to the Presidency of Serbia, the Federal Presidency of Yugoslavia, the republican and federal ministries of justice, and to the VJ. It was also given to Serbian and Albanian-language media in Kosovo. Critically, Your Honours, Lukic knew that these crimes were driving hundreds of thousands Kosovo Albanians from their homes. On September 23rd, 1998, for example, the Security Council noted that it was "gravely concerned" about "the excessive and indiscriminate use of force by Serbian security forces and the Yugoslav army," which according to the Secretary-General's estimates had resulted in the displacement of more than 230.000 persons from their homes. That's at Volume I, para 916; that's also at Volume III, paragraph 443 and at 677. The Chamber found that Lukic was aware of these allegations; that's at Volume III, paragraph 1120. He was present at a Joint Command meeting in which this resolution was discussed; that's Volume III, para 677. Based on the events of 1998 then, Lukic knew that he could count on the joint MUP-VJ operations to expel hundreds of thousands more Kosovo Albanians from their homes in 1999. That he continued to co-ordinate these same operations using these same troops to execute the campaign of terror and violence in 1999, the campaign at the heart of this JCE, Your Honours, shows that he intended to achieve the same results: The massive displacement and forcible transfer of Kosovo Albanians. Now, to be clear, Your Honours, contrary to the submission of my learned colleagues this morning, the Chamber did not rely solely on evidence from 1998 to determine Lukic's intent in 1999. In concluding that Lukic shared the common criminal purpose of the joint criminal enterprise, the Chamber relied on the totality of the evidence, including his continuing MUP-VJ crimes in 1999 -- his knowledge of continuing crimes in 1999. So let's look at that. The Chamber found the MUP staff received a steady stream of reports in 1999, including from 24 March 1999; that's at Volume III, para 1089. And this is a finding that's confirmed by information included in Lukic's own orders and reports. For example, on the 15th of April, 1999, Lukic issued a dispatch noting that some of his MUP intermediate commanders were "tolerating massive scale departures of civilian population." That's a finding at Volume III, paragraph 1094. And on the 4th of May, 1999, Lukic attended a meeting at a villa in Belgrade at which information was presented that the security forces of the VJ had dealt with numerous cases of violence, killings, pillage, and other crimes. He included information from this meeting in an order to his subordinates; that's at Volume III, para 1095. The Chamber will recall of course that as a JCE member, the crimes of the VJ are attributable to General Lukic; that's at Volume III, para 1132. Not only that, Your Honours, but crimes were often discussed at MUP staff meetings in 1999 as noted at paragraph 1126 of Volume III of the judgement. So as in 1998, in 1999 Lukic was informed of the massive displacement of Kosovo Albanians. For example, he reported on May 1st, 1999, that "between 24 March and 30 April 1999 a total of 715.158 persons belonging to the Siptar national minority left the territory ..." and that's a finding that's contained in a lot of the citations I mentioned at the beginning of my presentation. That's also specifically at Exhibit P1693. So under these circumstances, Your Honours, the Chamber properly found that Lukic, along with Sainovic and Pavkovic, intended the forcible displacements, including deportation and forcible transfer, that occurred during the indictment period. It was also reasonable to conclude that under these circumstances, Lukic's orders admonishing his subordinates to not commit crimes could not have been genuine as they found at Volume III, para 1129. Turning then to Your Honours' eighth question relating to JCE III, which is, for the sake of clarity of the record: "Discuss, with reference to the record, whether there would be any effect on Lukic's appeal regarding his convictions pursuant to JCE III, if the Appeals Chamber were to accept the Prosecution's argument that the Trial Chamber applied an incorrect mens rea standard for JCE III liability." The answer to this question, Your Honours, is that there would be no effect. As my colleagues have already explained in their responses to the appeals of Sainovic and to Pavkovic, the Trial Chamber here applied an incorrect and more restrictive probability standard in assessing JCE III liability -- JCE foreseeability, I'm sorry, rather than the correct and less-restrictive possibility standard from para 365 of the Brdjanin appeal judgement, paragraph 33 of the Blaskic appeal judgement, as affirmed by the Appeals Chamber in the 25 June 2009 decision on Prosecution's motion appealing Trial Chamber's decision on JCE III foreseeability from the Karadzic case. So in General Lukic's case then, the same findings that show that he knew that murder and destruction would probably be committed in the execution of the campaign of terror and violence also show that he knew that murder and destruction as acts of persecution were a possible consequence of the execution of this campaign. And those findings, for your reference, are at paragraphs 1134 and 1136 of Volume III of the trial judgement. Now, in his appeal, Lukic seems to be arguing that the Appeals Chamber should apply an even higher certainty standard by arguing that he cannot be convicted of crimes for which he had no knowledge. For example, in his challenge to his JCE III convictions for his -- for the murders in Djakovica, he argues there is no evidence that he "personally knew" of the murders or of the efforts to conceal the bodies afterwards, and that's at his brief in paragraph 700. The question, Your Honours, is not whether he knew of these crimes, but whether it was foreseeable to him that they were a possible consequence of the execution of the JCE of which he was a member. And that concludes my answer to the eighth question, Your Honours. I'll turn then to a few minor points. I see you have a question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Concerning with the murder in Djakovica, I would like to know if the victims are combatants or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber found that -- without the references to the trial judgement at hand, Your Honour, the Chamber found that those -- that constituted an act of persecution that was foreseeable to him and that resulted in his conviction of JCE III. Therefore, it follows that the victims of the murders in Djakovica were civilians, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So turning briefly then to the matter of Exhibit 6D614, which Judge T asked about this morning. Since it came up as a question, I'll address that briefly. The Trial Chamber properly exercised its discretion in denying admission of this 789-page document, where it found that the document lacked sufficient indicia of reliability to be tendered from the bar table as hearsay evidence. Now, as counsel for General Lukic mentioned this morning, it was a summary of documents. The underlying documents were not put before the Trial Chamber, so the Trial Chamber found it could not assess the accuracy of these summaries. Counsel for General Lukic today has failed, as he has in his brief, to explain how the Chamber abused its discretion under these circumstances and how this decision has had any impact on the judgement or his conviction. And I could refer Your Honours to the decision on this point of 2 July 2008 of the Trial Chamber; that's paragraphs 27 to 31. We also address this in our brief as well, Your Honours. In summation, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber properly convicted Lukic of deportation, inhumane acts, murder, and persecutions. His challenges in his appeal express his profound disagreement with the Trial Chamber's findings, but they fail to show any error. The Appeals Chamber should dismiss General Lukic's appeal, it should affirm his convictions, and it should adjust his sentence in accordance with the Prosecution appeal. And before I sit down, Your Honours, I do have a couple of corrections for earlier transcript references, specifically today's temporary transcript page 54, line 18, it reads "945, 1050," that should be "945 through 1050." And at transcript 61 of the temporary transcript today at line 13 it reads "the majority of the non-Albanian population was not part of the KLA," that should read "the majority of the Albanian population was not part of the KLA." And, Your Honours, Mr. President, in reference to your question about Djakovica, I would refer you to Volume II, paragraphs 1197 to 1198 for information about the Djakovica murders. And I can mention briefly that we won't be addressing sentencing today, Your Honours. The Prosecution's view is that General Lukic's sentence was too short, as has been argued in our appeal. You'll hear more about that tomorrow. And unless there's further questions, I'll conclude, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me there's no questions from the Bench at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that concludes the response from the Prosecution; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is, Your Honours, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The first thing that I have to say is that the Prosecution response seems to just rely on paragraphs from the judgement instead of the evidence. This is insufficient at this stage where the judgement is challenged. The OTP has no answer for our arguments that portions of the judgement are in contradiction with one another. What is their position as to the finding of mitigation evidence on the one hand and then the negation of the same in the same judgement? What is their position of the disparate treatment between other appellants and Lukic? Simply, the Prosecution would like to ignore findings that are not favourable to them, but a judgement cannot be read that way on appeal. If a judgement cannot stand on its own due to contradictions, it is unsafe and must be reviewed. The Prosecution has not and cannot rebut the clear error as to mitigation evidence from the judgement that we have summarised and presented for you. The judgement must be reversed for this reason on its own. Moving along further. The Prosecution says we have not changed our arguments, the factual story is the same as at trial. Well, how on earth how could it be changed? I don't understand what they're talking about. Obviously the evidence cannot be changed by either party, and we stand by our position that the evidence at trial, just as now, does not support the findings in the judgement and that acquittal is appropriate. Your Honours asked the Prosecution to provide specific reference to paragraphs of the judgement as to the question relating to evidence of Sreten Lukic's involvement in the disarming of the population. Throughout the rest of their response, all they did was cite paragraphs from the judgement. But for this specific request, they did not give you citations to the judgement. This highlights the error of the judgement as I detailed for you earlier today. You need to recall at this time that the voluntary surrender of arms were under way, was a time when all parties were working on peace accords. This is the area -- the time-period known as the October Accords when there were multiple peace initiatives in play, and peace, not war, were on everyone's mind. The items on the list that my colleague, Ms. Kravetz, presented to you are the same entries that I highlighted for you in my presentation, and every single one of them is related to the voluntary surrender of arms during this time-period when peace was on everyone's mind. Does that mean then that the UN and international mediators were also part of the JCE? We presented Lukic's only role was in relation to providing statistics to both Serb officials on the one hand and international officials, like Shaun Byrnes, on the other hand as to voluntary surrender of arms. Surely that is not to be viewed as a crime. In the context of arming, the Prosecution brought up the RPO, and I'd like to take a look at what that actually is and what Lukic's role is in relation to this topic. P2166 is the meeting in Belgrade that was cited to by the Prosecution. This document shows an important fact. It demonstrates that the Supreme Defence Council on June 9th, 1998, brought a decision based on the Law of the VJ, the Law on Defence, and the rules and regulations of the VJ to prepare a global plan for the suppression of terrorism which foresaw the engagement of the VJ and the MUP. If one looks at the evidence that was presented at trial, part 4 of this plan, this global plan, establishes the RPO. Again, this is the same plan that you heard of this morning during my presentation, where the Trial Chamber rightly concluded that neither the MUP nor Lukic participated in its drafting. This is at book III, paragraphs 1021. Further, the Prosecution did not provide any citations to any evidence demonstrating that a single crime from the indictment was committed by members of the RPO. Your Honours, I invite you to look at the evidence of -- the record of evidence because there has been no presentation of any such evidence. Again, one has to look at time-periods because the different time-periods that are at issue involved different legal frameworks, different factual frameworks, and they provide a totality of the evidence. The judgement at book I, paragraph 776, confirms that when the war began, when the NATO bombing began, these very same RPO were at that time mobilised and absorbed into their war time positions within the various defence structures of the state, whether the VJ, the MUP, civil protection, wherever their war time assignments were, they were absorbed into them. In book I, paragraph 788, as to the remaining 6.000 RPO that did not have a war time assignment, the Chamber concludes that they fell under the authority and command of the army, including in carrying out assignments relating to combat and that this was in accord with the Law of Defence, Articles 62 and 63. And for Your Honours's reference, the Law of Defence is P985 in evidence. So under the trial judgement's own conclusions, what could Lukic's involvement, authority, and purported command over these RPO amount to? It cannot. The Prosecution is avoiding dealing with the fact that there are different periods with different legal frameworks that cover the facts that were adduced at trial. Further on the issue of the RPO, counsel mentioned book III, paragraph 1066, and identified three documents - they are P1989, P1996, and 6D802 - as relating to Lukic's orders to RPO in actions. I urge the members of this panel to review all of those items because we submit that neither that paragraph of the judgement, nor the three documents cited, relate to any anti-terrorist actions or combat or anything of the sort in relation to the RPO. From this we see that the Prosecution has misrepresented the relevance of the RPO to Lukic and his authority over the same. I'd like to now turn to Lukic's interview which was also cited by the Prosecution in their response. Your Honours will recall that we have a separate ground of appeal relating to errors that arise from Mr. Lukic's interview and the manner that it was used in the trial, problems with the translations, and problems with the same. That is our ground F of the appellant's brief. I will not repeat all those arguments. I will just highlight something for you. The Prosecution's focus is on one particular selection that talks about the dual role as to the PJP of the staff, and again they seem to ignore different time-periods, just as the Chamber does at paragraph [sic] 3, 1013. In that paragraph, the Chamber also focuses on this same selection from the interview. What is ignored is that in this period, that is, 1999, Obrad Stevanovic, the commander of the PJP units and also the chief of the police administration within the MUP was on the ground in Kosovo. He didn't have an office. He used the staff. So when Lukic is talking about the MUP staff, you have to take into account that Obrad Stevanovic when he's in Kosovo, when he's in Pristina, he's at the MUP staff. Furthermore, as to the role that Lukic himself played, it's key to look at P948, which is his interview, and to look at several points in that interview, including at pages 4, pages 66, and pages 153, when Lukic says: I want to give you more details and explain to you the precise role of the MUP staff. And each time the Prosecution interviewer says: No, no, we'll get to that later, we'll get to that later, let's finish this. And he's never given a chance to give a full account, a full explanation, explaining precisely what the meaning of those words were, what the meaning of the MUP staff in the greater picture of things in the MUP hierarchy was, and what his role as head of staff was. That would conclude my comments as to the interview. I'd like to now move to the September -- excuse me, 17 February meeting that both Ms. Kravetz and Mr. Wood have referred to in their remarks. We have a fundamental problem -- or, I should say, the Prosecution and the Chamber have a fundamental problem that now is imputed to all of us. They are operating from the English translation of this document, which is not in comport -- does not comport to the B/C/S original of the document. So I would like to, with the indulgence of the interpreters, try to read the B/C/S original and see if we can obtain a translation of what is actually said in the minutes of that meeting. And I will now begin in B/C/S: [Interpretation] "The staff has planned to carry out, whenever this is ordered, three operations: Mopping-up of the terrain from the terrorists in the sectors of Podujevo, Dragobilje, and Drenica." [In English] And this is P1990 for the record. What is clear from the context of these words is not that the staff has planned an action, but rather that the staff is planning to carry out something once it is ordered, that it intends to carry out orders once they have given. The Prosecution has also mentioned and during this same time-period indeed dated, I believe, one day prior is P2808, which is an order from the Pristina Corps dealing with these exact same locations that are mentioned here, identifying both VJ and MUP units to be involved, and setting out assignments for the same. So indeed, the role of the MUP staff in this is not of the command nature that the Prosecution has implied. Now, I submit to you that both the judgement and the Prosecution ignore the facts on the ground as to 1999 and the evidence of the same, and I'd like to draw Your Honours' attention to some of those factors that I think are relevant for understanding this case. We have the testimony of Colonel Crosland, an international diplomat, that during this time-period the KLA controlled 70 per cent of the territory of Kosovo; that's at transcript page 9910. At the same time, NATO was bombing Kosovo every day and in evidence we had several incidents where NATO bombed Kosovo Albanian refugees. We also had several incidents where NATO bombs fell on civilian targets. We can call it something nice. We can call it collateral damage, but for people on the ground looking at their neighbours' houses being bombed they're thinking of it differently, they're thinking of it as a signal to get out of there before it's their house. Per Sandra Mitchell at transcript page 566 through 567, the Kosovo Verification Mission had evidence that 100.000 Serbs left their homes in Kosovo during the NATO bombing. That would amount to 40 per cent of the Serb population of Kosovo leaving during the NATO bombings. The figures given for the Kosovo Albanians leaving is 30 per cent of the Kosovo Albanian population. I think the question we all have to ask and which the Trial Chamber failed to ask: Were Serbs leaving their homes in Kosovo for the same reasons as the Albanians? A reasonable alternative reading of the evidence is that they were, that they were all leaving because of the NATO bombings, not the actions of the VJ or the MUP. Without an analysis to exclude that reasonable alternative conclusion, the Trial Chamber judgement is in error. I urge you to look at the evidence in the judgement that has now been relied upon, the paragraphs that have been relied upon by the Prosecution as to why people left, paragraph 1125, no citations to the evidence, that's in Volume II; Volume III, paragraph 45, again no citations to the evidence; paragraph 95, no numbers; paragraph 1123, no numbers, no citations to the evidence. The Trial Chamber did not calculate the number of departures that resulted from any direct evidence of expulsions of the type that are alleged in the Prosecution's indictment. There is no evidence-based findings on the number of persons expelled, nor the reasons why they left. If one looks at the witnesses that came and testified, there were 48 crime base witnesses. Thirty-three of the same, which amounts to 70 per cent, did not say that they left because they were forced out by the VJ and the MUP, but rather they said they left for other reasons like fears of NATO bombing, fears of combat between the KLA and the Yugoslav forces, or personal reasons. Those are legitimate reasons for people to leave. Those are similar legitimate reasons that people in other cases have been acquitted, like the Gotovina appeals judgement. Here we have direct evidence from Bislim Zyrapi, who was the KLA commander, who testified here at transcript page 6003, who confirmed that KLA ordered Kosovo Albanians to leave their homes as part of their plan and strategy. How can we, therefore, then exclude this as a reason for the displacements of persons that we saw? A reasonable Trial Chamber cannot, and therefore this judgement is in error. It is unsafe. One last topic I'd like to touch upon that my colleague Mr. Wood mentioned. In relation to notice of crimes, he gave us a reference to a paragraph and talking about Shaun Byrnes and what Shaun Byrnes said about the police burning homes on a daily basis. I'd like to look at what the evidence says, not what the trial judgement says. Shaun Byrnes at transcript page 12148: "I did not see a single PJP officer pull a trigger. I did not see a PJP officer light a house on fire by whatever means, but there were no Albanians about. They had fled and the village was in flames." Under this evidence it is not the only reasonable conclusion that crimes imputed to the MUP can be inferred. People flee and houses burn from legitimate combat as well. The biggest problem with the OTP and the judgement is they forget or fail to apply the principle of in dubio pro reo throughout and that is the single most reason why, Your Honours, your review is required and why this judgement is unsafe, illogical, and must be overturned. And I thank you for the time to make these submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that there's no questions from the Bench, so that concludes the hearings for today. And tomorrow we'll have a longer day. We'll start from 9.00 until 5.00, compared with today -- yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have one further transcript correction to make, just for the clarity of the record. At transcript 70, line 3, today it says the number "78" but it should really be line "1178" which is what I intended to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
